title: Value-Based Care: From Fee-for-Service to Outcomes
subtitle: ACOs, bundled payments, quality measures, risk adjustment, and the future of healthcare payment
description: A comprehensive course on the transformation of healthcare payment from volume to value. Covers the failures of fee-for-service, the logic and mechanics of ACOs and bundled payments, how quality is measured and tied to payment, risk adjustment, Star Ratings, and where the field is heading. Essential for anyone in health system finance, clinical leadership, managed care, or policy.
targetAudience: Health system finance and strategy staff
Policy analysts and health reform advocates

lessons.title: Why Fee-for-Service Fails: Incentives & Consequences
lessons.summary: How fee-for-service payment creates perverse incentives, drives overutilization, fragments care, and contributes to the US spending crisis.

objectives.text: Explain the core incentive problem in fee-for-service payment
Identify how FFS contributes to care fragmentation and overutilization
Describe the Dartmouth Atlas findings and their policy implications

contentBlocks.heading: Pay for doing, not for healing
contentBlocks.body:
Fee-for-service (FFS) is simple: providers are paid a fee for each service they deliver. An office visit, a lab test, an MRI, a surgical procedure — each generates a separate payment. The more you do, the more you earn.

The problem is equally simple: in FFS, there is no payment for keeping patients healthy, no payment for coordinating care across providers, no payment for avoiding unnecessary procedures, and no penalty for poor outcomes. A hospital that reduces its readmission rate loses revenue. A primary care physician who prevents a hospitalization earns nothing for that prevention. The system pays for activity, not results.

contentBlocks.heading: The Dartmouth finding: geography is destiny
contentBlocks.body:
In the 1990s, researchers at Dartmouth Medical School published the Dartmouth Atlas of Health Care — a landmark analysis showing that Medicare spending per beneficiary varied by more than 2:1 across US regions, with no correlation to health outcomes. Patients in high-spending regions did not live longer or report better health than patients in low-spending regions.

The implication was explosive: a huge share of US healthcare spending was not buying health. It was buying more services — more tests, more specialist visits, more days in the hospital — that delivered no measurable benefit to patients.

contentBlocks.heading: The coordination failure
contentBlocks.body: In a pure FFS world, a diabetic patient may see a primary care physician, an endocrinologist, a cardiologist, a nephrologist, and a podiatrist — each billing independently, each with their own records, none responsible for the whole person. No one is paid to make sure all five providers are working toward a coherent plan. This fragmentation produces redundant testing, conflicting medications, and preventable hospitalizations.

lessons.title: RVUs: How Physician Payment Works — and Why It Favors Procedures
lessons.summary: The Resource-Based Relative Value Scale, how RVUs translate to physician pay, why cognitive primary care is systematically undervalued, and CMS efforts to rebalance.

objectives.text: Explain how the RBRVS and RVU system determine physician payment in Medicare
Describe why the RVU system systematically undervalues cognitive primary care relative to procedures
Explain the role of the AMA RVS Update Committee (RUC) in setting RVU values

contentBlocks.heading: One number drives most of physician pay
contentBlocks.body:
Medicare pays physicians based on the Resource-Based Relative Value Scale (RBRVS). Every covered service has a Relative Value Unit (RVU) value — a number representing the relative resource intensity of that service. Multiply the RVU by the national conversion factor (~$33 in 2024) and you get the Medicare payment.

A 99213 (brief office visit) is worth about 1.3 RVUs → ~$43. A 99214 (moderate office visit) is 1.92 RVUs → ~$63. A knee arthroscopy is 10+ RVUs → $340+. A primary care physician seeing 20 patients per day at 1–2 RVUs each earns less than a surgeon doing three procedures.

contentBlocks.heading: The RUC: specialty-dominated valuation
contentBlocks.body: RVU values are recommended by the AMA/Specialty Society Relative Value Scale Update Committee (RUC) — a 29-member body historically dominated by specialists. Primary care has consistently argued the RUC undervalues cognitive work (thinking, coordinating, managing complexity) and overvalues procedural skills. MedPAC has repeatedly found that primary care RVUs are too low, contributing to the primary care–specialty income gap of more than $100,000 annually.

lessons.title: MIPS: The Merit-Based Incentive Payment System
lessons.summary: How MIPS adjusts Medicare physician payment based on quality, cost, clinical improvement activities, and promoting interoperability — and why many argue it's not true value-based care.

objectives.text: Describe the four performance categories in MIPS and their weights
Explain how MIPS payment adjustments work
Articulate why critics argue MIPS fails to deliver true value-based care transformation

contentBlocks.heading: MACRA and the end of the SGR
contentBlocks.body:
The Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act (MACRA, 2015) repealed the sustainable growth rate (SGR) formula — which had created annual payment cliff-hangers for a decade — and replaced it with two pathways: the Merit-Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) and Advanced APMs.

MIPS adjusts physician Medicare payments based on composite performance. A physician scoring above the performance threshold earns a positive adjustment (up to +9%); below threshold earns a negative adjustment (up to -9%). Most physicians participate in MIPS rather than an Advanced APM.

contentBlocks.heading: MIPS four performance categories

items.title: Quality (30%)
items.body: Reports on 6 quality measures selected from a menu. Compared to national benchmarks. Most measures can be gamed by selecting easy ones.

items.title: Cost (30%)
items.body: CMS calculates total resource use and episode costs from claims — physician doesn't report, CMS attributes. Higher weight added in recent years.

items.title: Improvement Activities (15%)
items.body: Activities like care coordination, beneficiary engagement, patient safety. Checked off rather than measured — widely criticized as box-checking.

items.title: Promoting Interoperability (25%)
items.body: Use of certified EHR technology, e-prescribing, patient access APIs. Rewards EHR adoption and usage.

contentBlocks.heading: Why MIPS isn't really value-based care
contentBlocks.body: MIPS adjusts payment at the margins (±9%) on top of the existing FFS rate — it doesn't change the fundamental incentive structure. A physician who sees more patients still earns more. MedPAC, CMS's own advisory body, recommended repealing MIPS and replacing it with population-based payment models. In 2023, MedPAC called MIPS a 'check-the-box exercise' that doesn't meaningfully change care delivery.

questions.question: What is the maximum positive payment adjustment a physician can receive under MIPS?
questions.explanation: MIPS payment adjustments range from -9% (lowest performers) to +9% (highest performers), applied to a physician's Medicare payments for the performance year.

lessons.title: Why the Way We Pay for Healthcare Is Breaking the System — And How Paying for Value Could Fix It
lessons.summary: The United States spends more on healthcare than any nation on earth — yet ranks 37th in health outcomes. This module explains why that paradox exists, how the fee-for-service payment system created it, and how value-based care offers a fundamentally different path forward.

objectives.text: Explain the US healthcare spending paradox using current data
Describe how fee-for-service payment works and the perverse incentives it creates
Define value-based care and distinguish it from fee-for-service
Identify the four main categories of value-based payment models
Explain why Vermont is a national leader in the shift to value-based care

contentBlocks.body:
Imagine paying a mechanic every time they touched your car — whether or not it ran better afterward. Now imagine that mechanic's salary depended entirely on how many parts they replaced, not on whether your car actually worked. You would quickly end up with a very expensive car that still broke down constantly. This, in essence, is how the United States pays for healthcare.

The US spent $4.5 trillion on healthcare in 2022 — roughly $13,493 per person, and 18.3 percent of the entire national economy. That is more than any other high-income country, by a wide margin. Switzerland, the second-highest spender, dedicates about 11.3 percent of its GDP to health. Germany spends 12.8 percent. Canada spends 12.2 percent.

And yet — despite outspending every peer nation — the US ranks 37th in overall health outcomes according to the World Health Organization. Americans live shorter lives than citizens of 40 other countries. The US infant mortality rate is nearly double that of Finland. Preventable deaths from conditions like diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease occur at far higher rates here than in comparable wealthy nations.

contentBlocks.heading: How Did We Get Here? Understanding Fee-for-Service
contentBlocks.body: To understand why America spends so much and gets so little, you need to understand the payment system that drives almost every clinical decision made in the country. That system is called fee-for-service, often abbreviated FFS. Fee-for-service has been the dominant payment model for American medicine since the mid-20th century.

contentBlocks.heading: Key Concept
contentBlocks.body: Fee-for-Service (FFS): A payment model in which healthcare providers are paid separately for each service they deliver — each office visit, each test, each procedure, each hospital day. Payment is triggered by doing something, not by whether the patient gets better.

Here is how it works in practice: a physician, hospital, or other provider submits a claim to an insurer — Medicare, Medicaid, or a private insurer — using standardized billing codes called CPT codes. Each code corresponds to a specific service: a visit, a blood draw, an MRI, a surgical procedure. The insurer reviews the claim and pays a set rate for each code. The provider's revenue depends entirely on how many services they bill, not on whether those services helped the patient.

contentBlocks.heading: The Perverse Incentives of Fee-for-Service
contentBlocks.body:
The word 'perverse' in economics means an incentive that pushes behavior in the opposite direction from what you actually want. Fee-for-service is full of perverse incentives. Consider what happens when a hospital successfully reduces readmissions by improving care coordination after discharge. Under fee-for-service, that hospital just reduced its own revenue — because each readmission generates thousands of dollars in billing.

Or consider preventive care. A primary care physician who spends an extra 30 minutes helping a diabetic patient understand diet, exercise, and medication adherence may prevent that patient from ever needing a $50,000 hospitalization. Under fee-for-service, the physician is paid a modest office visit fee for those 30 minutes. The hospital that would have done the expensive hospitalization loses revenue. The system as a whole saves money — but the individual providers doing the right thing are financially worse off.

contentBlocks.heading: Note
contentBlocks.body: Under fee-for-service, prevention is a cost center, not a revenue source. Providers are paid to treat illness, not to prevent it. This single fact explains more about America's healthcare crisis than almost any other.

contentBlocks.heading: Defining Value-Based Care: A Fundamentally Different Approach
contentBlocks.body: Value-based care, sometimes called value-based payment or value-based purchasing, is a healthcare delivery and payment model in which providers are paid based on patient health outcomes rather than the volume of services provided. The key word is 'value' — defined in healthcare as the quality of care delivered divided by the cost of delivering it.

contentBlocks.heading: Key Concept
contentBlocks.body: Value-Based Care: A payment and delivery model where providers earn more when they keep patients healthier, improve quality, and reduce unnecessary costs — and earn less when they deliver high volumes of low-quality or unnecessary care. The core formula: Value = Quality / Cost.

This seems like a simple idea — pay for results, not for activity. But implementing it requires solving genuinely hard problems: How do you measure quality? How do you attribute outcomes to specific providers when patients see many doctors? How do you prevent providers from avoiding sick patients to protect their quality scores? How do you account for the fact that some patients have more complex needs than others? These are the questions that value-based payment models are designed to address.

contentBlocks.heading: The Four Main Categories of Value-Based Payment Models
contentBlocks.body: Value-based care is not a single payment model — it is a family of models that shift payment from volume to value in different ways and to different degrees. Think of a spectrum: at one end is pure fee-for-service with no accountability for outcomes; at the other end is full capitation where providers take on complete financial responsibility for a population's health. Most VBC models sit somewhere in between.

contentBlocks.heading: Category 1: Pay-for-Performance
contentBlocks.body: Pay-for-performance (P4P) is the simplest form of value-based payment. Providers still get paid fee-for-service for each service, but they receive bonuses for hitting quality targets — or face penalties for missing them. Examples include CMS's Hospital Value-Based Purchasing program, which adjusts Medicare payments to hospitals based on quality scores, and the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) for physicians.

contentBlocks.heading: Category 2: Accountable Care Organizations and Shared Savings
contentBlocks.body:
Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) are networks of doctors, hospitals, and other providers that work together to coordinate care for a defined group of patients. The ACO is given a benchmark spending target. If the ACO spends less than the benchmark while maintaining quality, it shares in those savings. This model keeps the fee-for-service billing infrastructure but adds accountability for total cost of care.

Medicare ACOs generated $1.87 billion in net savings for Medicare in 2022, according to CMS. As of 2024, more than 480 ACOs participate in the Medicare Shared Savings Program, covering over 11 million beneficiaries. Vermont's OneCare Vermont is an ACO that serves both Medicare and Medicaid populations — and is the centerpiece of the state's nationally recognized All-Payer Model.

contentBlocks.heading: Category 3: Bundled Payments
contentBlocks.body: Bundled payments group all the costs for a single episode of care — say, a hip replacement surgery plus the 90 days of recovery — into one fixed payment. All providers involved must share that single payment. If they deliver great care efficiently and spend less than the bundle price, they keep the difference. If they spend more, they lose money. This directly incentivizes coordination across the care team.

contentBlocks.heading: Category 4: Capitation and Global Budgets
contentBlocks.body: Capitation is the most fundamental shift: providers receive a fixed monthly payment per patient to cover all their care, regardless of how many services that patient uses. The provider takes on complete financial responsibility — called full risk — for the patient's health. If the patient stays healthy and uses few services, the provider keeps the surplus. Global budgets take this idea to the health-system level: an entire hospital or health system receives a fixed annual budget to care for a defined population.

contentBlocks.heading: Vermont: A National Laboratory for Value-Based Care
contentBlocks.body:
Vermont is the only state in the nation operating an approved All-Payer Accountable Care Organization Model — a program that brings Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance under a single set of quality and spending targets for the first time in American history. This makes Vermont uniquely important to anyone studying value-based care. What Vermont learns, the nation watches.

The Vermont All-Payer ACO Model was approved by CMS in 2016 and launched in January 2017. At its center is OneCare Vermont, a statewide ACO that contracts with hospitals, physicians, and community organizations across the state. OneCare Vermont currently serves approximately 240,000 Vermonters — nearly 40 percent of the state's population — through its attributed beneficiary program.

contentBlocks.heading: The Green Mountain Care Board
contentBlocks.body:
Vermont's All-Payer Model is overseen by the Green Mountain Care Board (GMCB), a state agency with broad authority to regulate healthcare costs, review hospital budgets, and set statewide health spending targets. The GMCB is one of the most powerful state-level healthcare cost-control bodies in the nation. It reviews and approves hospital budgets every year — meaning hospitals cannot simply raise prices without regulatory approval.

This combination — a statewide ACO (OneCare Vermont) operating under regulatory oversight (GMCB), with a federal partnership (CMS All-Payer Model) — makes Vermont's healthcare system genuinely unique. Understanding how it works, and why it was designed this way, is one of the most valuable things you can learn if you work in Vermont healthcare.

contentBlocks.heading: Why This Matters to You, Wherever You Work
contentBlocks.body:
If you are a nurse, this transformation changes what your work looks like. Value-based care prioritizes care coordination, discharge planning, chronic disease management, and patient education — all activities that nurses are uniquely positioned to lead. Under fee-for-service, a nurse who prevented a readmission by spending extra time on discharge education was not generating revenue. Under VBC, that same nurse is helping the organization succeed financially.

If you are a hospital administrator, VBC means thinking differently about your budget. Revenue is no longer simply a function of volume. Quality scores, total cost of care for your population, and care coordination infrastructure become central financial drivers. Understanding which patients are at highest risk of expensive preventable events — and investing in keeping them well — becomes essential to financial sustainability.

contentBlocks.heading: What You Will Learn in This Course
contentBlocks.body:
This course has six modules, each building on the last. Module 2 dives into the economics: how money flows through the healthcare system and the mechanics of each major payment model in depth. Module 3 focuses on clinical practice: how VBC changes the daily reality of delivering care. Module 4 examines the policy landscape: the federal programs and Vermont-specific structures that govern the transition. Module 5 covers technology: the data infrastructure that makes VBC possible. Module 6 addresses the most urgent challenge: health equity, and how VBC can be designed to reduce — rather than worsen — the disparities that exist in every healthcare system.

By the end of this course, you will have a sophisticated understanding of one of the most consequential transformations happening in American healthcare. You will understand not just what value-based care is, but why it was designed the way it is, how it plays out in real clinical settings, and what it means for patients, providers, and communities across Vermont and the nation.

contentBlocks.heading: Quote
contentBlocks.body: The question is no longer whether healthcare should move to value-based payment — it is how fast and how completely. Every major payer, every major health system, and every serious policymaker now agrees that fee-for-service as the dominant payment model is unsustainable. The only debate is about the pace and mechanics of transition.

tracks.description: How ACOs align provider incentives around total cost of care and quality, the MSSP program, and the evidence on ACO performance.

lessons.title: ACO Fundamentals: Attribution, Benchmarks & Shared Savings
lessons.summary: How ACOs work: patient attribution, spending benchmarks, shared savings and losses, and the Medicare Shared Savings Program structure.

objectives.text: Explain the three core mechanics of ACO payment: attribution, benchmark, shared savings
Describe the difference between one-sided and two-sided risk
Explain how MSSP tracks are structured and how they create a glide path to risk

contentBlocks.heading: The ACO concept: accountability for a population
contentBlocks.body:
An Accountable Care Organization is a group of providers — typically a network of primary care physicians, specialists, and often a hospital — that agrees to take joint accountability for the cost and quality of care for an attributed population.

ACOs do not change how patients access care. There are no locked networks, no referral requirements for patients. Patients continue to see their regular doctors. But behind the scenes, those doctors now have financial stakes in the total cost of all care their patients receive — wherever they receive it.

contentBlocks.heading: The three core mechanics

items.title: Attribution
items.body: CMS assigns Medicare beneficiaries to an ACO based on where they receive the plurality of their primary care. Patients don't choose an ACO — they are assigned.

items.title: Benchmark
items.body: CMS calculates what it would have spent on the ACO's attributed population without the ACO, based on historical spending and trend. This is the benchmark — the spending target.

items.title: Shared savings/losses
items.body: If the ACO spends below its benchmark and meets quality thresholds, it earns a share of the savings. If it's in two-sided risk and overspends, it owes a share of the excess back.

contentBlocks.heading: One-sided vs. two-sided risk

rows.label: Savings sharing
rows.right: ACO keeps larger portion of savings

rows.label: Loss exposure
rows.left: ACO owes nothing if it overspends
rows.right: ACO owes portion of overspend back to CMS

contentBlocks.heading: MSSP: the Medicare ACO program
contentBlocks.body: The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP), created by the ACA in 2010, is the largest ACO program in the country. As of 2024, MSSP includes over 480 ACOs covering more than 10 million Medicare beneficiaries. CMS also runs REACH ACOs (formerly Direct Contracting), which take deeper risk with enhanced flexibility.

contentBlocks.label: ACO CFO perspective: managing total cost of care

lessons.title: ACO Performance: What the Evidence Shows
lessons.summary: A balanced look at ACO savings data, quality outcomes, which ACOs succeed and why, and the honest limitations of the model.

objectives.text: Summarize the evidence on MSSP ACO savings and quality performance
Identify the characteristics of high-performing ACOs
Explain the benchmark problem and why some argue early ACO savings were illusory

contentBlocks.heading: The overall scorecard
contentBlocks.body:
ACOs have produced meaningful but modest net savings. CMS data through 2023 shows MSSP ACOs generate gross savings of $2–3 billion annually, but after sharing those savings with ACOs, the net savings to Medicare are smaller — and varied by study design.

Quality performance has generally been positive: MSSP ACOs outperform FFS on preventive care measures, follow-up after hospitalization, and patient experience. High-performing ACOs consistently show improvements in diabetes management, hypertension control, and avoidable hospitalizations.

contentBlocks.heading: The benchmark problem
contentBlocks.body: A persistent criticism: MSSP benchmarks are based on each ACO's own historical spending. ACOs that were already efficient had low benchmarks — they had to become even more efficient to generate savings. Early ACO savings may have been driven partly by organizations that had been overspending entering the program and cutting waste, not structural transformation. CMS has moved to regional benchmarks to address this.

contentBlocks.heading: What high-performing ACOs do differently

items.title: Robust primary care
items.body: High-touch primary care with care managers embedded in practices, proactive outreach to high-risk patients, and after-hours access.

items.title: Behavioral health integration
items.body: Integrated behavioral health in primary care settings — addressing depression, substance use, and mental illness that drive high utilization.

items.title: Post-acute care management
items.body: Tight relationships with skilled nursing facilities, home health agencies, and hospitalists to reduce readmissions and optimize post-hospital care.

items.title: Data analytics
items.body: Real-time claims data to identify rising-risk patients before hospitalization. ACOs without analytics struggle to target interventions.

questions.question: Why did CMS move from historical to regional benchmarks for MSSP ACOs?
questions.explanation: Historical benchmarks penalized already-efficient ACOs (they had less room to cut) and rewarded previously high-spending organizations that had easy waste to eliminate. Regional benchmarks compare ACOs to peers in their market.

options.text: Regional benchmarks are easier to calculate and require less data
Historical benchmarks penalized efficient ACOs; regional benchmarks compare ACOs to their market peers
CMS was required by Congress to switch to regional benchmarks in the ACA
Regional benchmarks allow ACOs to earn more shared savings

lessons.title: ACOs Beyond Medicare: Medicaid and Commercial ACOs
lessons.summary: How ACO models have expanded into Medicaid and commercial markets — state-based ACO programs, multi-payer ACOs, and the structural differences from Medicare ACOs.

objectives.text: Describe how state Medicaid ACO programs differ from Medicare MSSP
Explain the multi-payer ACO model and its advantages
Identify Vermont's OneCare and Oregon's CCO as leading state ACO models

contentBlocks.heading: ACOs expanded beyond Medicare
contentBlocks.body: The MSSP ACO model was designed for traditional Medicare. But states and commercial payers have developed their own ACO-like models for Medicaid and commercial populations. The structure varies more widely — some use global budgets, some use shared savings, some are voluntary while others are mandatory for enrolled populations.

contentBlocks.heading: State ACO models: leading examples

items.title: Vermont — OneCare
items.body: Statewide ACO with global budget covering Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial lives. Participates in AHEAD model. Physicians choose to attribute patients.

items.title: Oregon — CCOs
items.body: Coordinated Care Organizations. Medicaid-only. Regional entities covering all Medicaid services including behavioral health and LTSS with global budget accountability.

items.title: Massachusetts — ACO model
items.body: MassHealth (Medicaid) ACO program. Accountable Care Partnership Plans and Primary Care ACO tracks. Among the largest and most evaluated Medicaid ACO programs.

items.title: North Carolina — Tailored Plans
items.body: Medicaid managed care with behavioral health ACO integration. Addresses social needs through community health workers and NCCARE360 referral platform.

contentBlocks.heading: Multi-payer alignment: why it matters
contentBlocks.body: A primary care practice participating in a Medicare ACO, a Medicaid ACO, and a commercial ACO simultaneously faces different attribution methodologies, different benchmarks, different quality measures, and different payment timelines from each. Multi-payer alignment — aligning these programs so one set of incentives points in the same direction — is the goal of models like AHEAD and Vermont's all-payer approach.

questions.question: What does 'multi-payer alignment' mean in the ACO context?
questions.explanation: Multi-payer alignment means coordinating ACO-type incentives across Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial payers so that providers receive consistent signals about quality and cost — rather than conflicting requirements from each payer.

options.text: Multiple ACOs working together in the same geographic area
Coordinating incentives across Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial payers toward the same goals
ACOs that accept patients from multiple states
Aligning physician and hospital payment within a single ACO

lessons.title: Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 3: The Economics Pillar — Following the Money in Value-Based Care
lessons.summary: Module 3 of the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course examines the financial mechanics of value-based care from first principles. It explains, in plain language, how money actually flows in the major VBC contract structures — shared savings, bundled payments, and capitation — how providers calculate whether a VBC arrangement is financially rational for their organization, what the volume-to-value transition problem means in practice for health system balance sheets, and what the economic evidence says about which VBC models generate durable savings versus which ones simply shift cost without reducing it. Learners will leave this module able to evaluate a VBC contract term sheet, identify the key actuarial concepts their finance teams are using, and understand the economic case for primary care investment as the highest-return infrastructure spend in healthcare.

Compare upside-only and two-sided risk tracks and identify the balance sheet conditions that determine which is appropriate.

contentBlocks.body: Here is a question that sounds simple but is genuinely hard to answer: if a hospital successfully reduces its patients’ hospitalization rate by 15% through better care management, is that good news or bad news for the hospital’s finances? The instinctive answer is that it must be good news — fewer hospitalizations means healthier patients, which is surely the goal. But in a world where 40% of that hospital’s revenue still comes from fee-for-service Medicare and Medicaid payments, fewer hospitalizations means fewer inpatient admissions, which means fewer billed days, which means lower revenue. The hospital just cut its own income by doing its job better. This is not a hypothetical paradox — it is the central economic tension of the volume-to-value transition, experienced by virtually every health system that has seriously engaged with value-based care. Understanding this tension, and the financial mechanisms that VBC contract structures use to resolve it, is what this module is about.

contentBlocks.heading: The Financial Anatomy of a Shared Savings Contract
contentBlocks.body:
The Medicare Shared Savings Program is the most widely adopted VBC model in the United States, and shared savings is the financial mechanism at its core. Understanding how shared savings actually works — how the benchmark is set, how savings are calculated, and how they are distributed — is the foundation for understanding the economics of most VBC arrangements. The concept is straightforward: CMS calculates how much it would have expected to spend on your attributed patient population if they had remained in traditional fee-for-service Medicare, adjusted for their age, health status, and geographic cost factors. This projected spend is your “benchmark.” If your ACO’s actual spending on that population comes in below the benchmark, the difference is “savings.” You share those savings with CMS according to a pre-agreed formula — typically retaining 40–75% depending on your risk track and quality performance, with CMS keeping the remainder.

The devil, as always, is in the details. The benchmark calculation uses a three-year historical average of your patient population’s spending, adjusted upward by a national trend factor. For ACOs whose patient populations were already low-cost before joining the program, this creates an immediate structural problem: their benchmark is low, so even excellent care management produces modest absolute savings, making the shared savings payment insufficient to cover the care management infrastructure investment. This is called the “low benchmark problem,” and it is the primary reason that rural and safety-net ACOs, which often already operate lean systems with lower baseline utilization, struggle to generate shared savings large enough to justify Advanced APM participation costs. CMS has modified the benchmark methodology three times since 2012 in response to this problem, most recently in the Pathways to Success Rule of 2018 and the 2023 ACO Primary Care Flex Model, but the fundamental tension between historical benchmarking and equitable VBC participation for already-efficient providers remains unresolved.

contentBlocks.heading: Upside-Only vs. Two-Sided Risk: The Decision That Changes Everything
contentBlocks.body:
One of the most consequential decisions a provider organization makes when entering a shared savings arrangement is whether to accept only upside risk — where you share in savings if you beat the benchmark but owe nothing if you miss it — or two-sided risk, where you both share savings and repay losses if spending exceeds the benchmark. This choice has profound implications for the financial planning, working capital requirements, and organizational risk appetite of the participating entity. Upside-only arrangements (MSSP Track 1 and its successors) are appropriate for organizations beginning their VBC journey: they provide financial experience with population cost management without the catastrophic downside scenario of a major loss repayment obligation. Two-sided arrangements (MSSP ENHANCED Track, Direct Contracting, ACO REACH) offer higher shared savings percentages — sometimes up to 80% of savings — but require the organization to maintain actuarial reserves sufficient to cover a loss scenario, typically modeled at 1–3% of benchmark spending.

The financial model in the table above illustrates why Two-Sided and Full-Risk tracks are substantially more attractive in their best-case financial outcome — but also why the actuarial reserve requirement creates a genuine barrier to entry for organizations operating at thin margins. For a health system with $30 million in unrestricted net assets, maintaining a $2.5 million actuarial reserve for ACO REACH participation represents a 8.3% allocation of available capital to a risk management buffer — a rational investment if leadership has high confidence in the organization’s ability to manage population cost, but a significant commitment that requires board-level approval and careful opportunity cost analysis against other capital needs.

contentBlocks.heading: Bundled Payments: When a Single Price Covers an Entire Episode of Care
contentBlocks.body:
Bundled payment models take a different economic approach to aligning incentives than shared savings. Rather than holding a provider accountable for the total cost of care across an entire attributed population, bundled payments establish a single target price for all the care associated with a specific clinical episode — typically defined as a procedure or hospitalization plus 90 days of post-acute care. If the sum of all actual payments during the episode falls below the target price, the lead provider (typically the hospital or physician group that performed the primary procedure) retains the difference. If actual costs exceed the target, the lead provider repays the excess. The economic logic is straightforward: bundled payments create a direct financial incentive for the hospital performing a hip replacement to care about which skilled nursing facility the patient is discharged to, how long they stay there, and whether they end up readmitted — because all of those costs are included in the bundle.

BPCI Advanced, CMS’s current bundled payment program, covers 32 clinical episodes ranging from major joint replacement and cardiac surgery to pneumonia and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease hospitalizations. The program has generated the strongest evidence of any CMS alternative payment model for procedural episodes: a 2024 CMS evaluation found that BPCI Advanced participants reduced episode spending by an average of $2,100 per episode for major joint replacement while maintaining or improving quality outcomes, generating net Medicare savings of $900 million between 2018 and 2023. Critically, these savings came primarily from reductions in post-acute care spending — fewer days in skilled nursing facilities and more patients discharged directly home with home health services — rather than from reductions in the procedural care itself, confirming the bundled payment hypothesis that the primary driver of unnecessary cost in high-volume procedures is the post-acute care tail, not the procedure.

contentBlocks.heading: Quote
contentBlocks.body: The bundled payment evidence for joint replacement is about as clean as healthcare economics gets: when you make the hospital financially responsible for what happens after the patient leaves, patients spend less time in nursing homes, have fewer complications, and cost Medicare significantly less money. The same logic applies to any high-volume procedure with a predictable post-acute care pattern. The challenge is applying it to medical conditions where the post-acute trajectory is far less predictable. — Leemore Dafny, Harvard Business School, Health Affairs, 2025.

contentBlocks.heading: Capitation: The Most Advanced — and Most Misunderstood — VBC Model
contentBlocks.body:
Capitation is the payment model that most completely aligns provider incentives with patient health outcomes, and the one that generates the most anxiety among providers who have not operated under it before. Under capitation, a provider or provider organization receives a fixed payment per enrolled member per month — the “PMPM” rate — and is responsible for delivering or arranging all covered healthcare services for that member, regardless of how much care they actually use. If the member uses more care than the PMPM covers, the provider absorbs the loss. If the member uses less, the provider retains the surplus. This structure creates the strongest possible financial incentive for prevention, care coordination, and early intervention — because every avoided hospitalization translates directly into retained revenue rather than lost fee-for-service income.

The anxiety around capitation is understandable but often misdirected. The concern most commonly expressed is that capitation incentivizes providers to withhold necessary care — to under-treat rather than over-treat. This concern is real and has historical basis: the managed care capitation models of the 1990s were frequently criticized for exactly this failure, and some HMO capitation arrangements did produce documented under-treatment in specific service categories. But the lesson of the 1990s HMO experience is not that capitation is inherently dangerous. It is that capitation without robust quality measurement, meaningful patient choice, and strong external accountability produces dangerous incentives. Modern capitation models — including Medicare Advantage plans and CMS’s ACO REACH program — include comprehensive quality metric frameworks with financial consequences for poor performance, minimum coverage requirements that prevent service restriction below evidence-based thresholds, and beneficiary rights to seek care outside the network when needed. The capitation model that exists in 2026 is substantively different from the managed care capitation of 1996.

contentBlocks.heading: How PMPM Rates Are Set: The Actuarial Core of Capitation
contentBlocks.body: The financial success or failure of a capitation arrangement is largely determined before any patient is seen, at the point where the PMPM rate is negotiated or set. If the rate is set too low relative to the actual cost of providing care to the enrolled population, no amount of care management efficiency will produce a viable financial model. If the rate is set appropriately — reflecting the health acuity, demographic profile, and social complexity of the enrolled population — a well-managed capitated provider can generate margins of 3–8% while delivering care that is demonstrably better in quality and lower in total cost than the fee-for-service alternative. The actuarial process of setting a PMPM rate involves risk adjustment models that account for enrollee diagnoses, functional status, and social determinants of health, applied to utilization cost data from comparable populations. For Medicare Advantage plans, CMS sets the base rate using the county-level fee-for-service benchmark and adjusts it upward or downward based on each enrollee’s Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) risk score, a diagnosis-based model that attempts to predict expected healthcare utilization for that individual in the coming year.

contentBlocks.heading: The Volume-to-Value Transition: Why the Math Gets Hard Before It Gets Easy
contentBlocks.body:
The single most common financial mistake health systems make in VBC transitions is underestimating the revenue disruption of the transition period — the window, typically 18 to 36 months, during which care management investments have begun reducing utilization but VBC contract revenue has not yet scaled to replace the lost fee-for-service volume. Consider a regional health system generating $400 million in annual net patient revenue, with 30% of that revenue from inpatient admissions billed on a fee-for-service basis. The system joins MSSP and invests $2 million in care management infrastructure — care coordinators, a risk stratification platform, a post-discharge follow-up program — that begins generating measurable results in year one, reducing its attributed Medicare population’s hospitalization rate by 12%. That 12% reduction represents approximately 240 avoided admissions. At an average net revenue of $8,500 per admission, it also represents a $2.04 million reduction in fee-for-service inpatient revenue. The system’s MSSP shared savings payment for year one, based on total population savings, might be $1.4 million. Net financial impact of year one VBC investment: negative $640,000.

This math is not an argument against VBC. It is an argument for understanding VBC as a multi-year financial investment with a specific payback horizon, rather than a year-one revenue enhancement strategy. The financial literature on mature ACO performance consistently shows that organizations reaching their fifth year of MSSP participation generate shared savings payments averaging $312 per attributed beneficiary annually, compared to an average investment cost of $87 per beneficiary in care management infrastructure — a return on investment of approximately 3.6 to 1. The problem is that most health system financial planning cycles operate on one-to-three year horizons, which are too short to capture the full economic benefit of VBC investment. Organizations that have successfully navigated the volume-to-value transition have done so by securing board approval for a five-to-seven year VBC investment thesis with explicit transition period loss projections, rather than attempting to justify each year’s VBC expenditure against that same year’s VBC revenue.

contentBlocks.heading: Key Concept
contentBlocks.body: For CFOs and Finance Leaders: If your organization is evaluating ACO or Advanced APM participation, your financial model must explicitly project the transition period revenue displacement — the reduction in fee-for-service inpatient and ED revenue that will occur as care management succeeds. An ACO financial model that shows positive net revenue in year one almost certainly has a methodology error, either in the care management cost estimates or in the assumed savings rate. Realistic five-year models typically show a cumulative loss in years one and two, breakeven in year three, and meaningful positive return in years four and five. Present this model honestly to your board, or the VBC investment will be defunded the first time a quarterly loss appears.

contentBlocks.heading: Primary Care Investment as Economic Infrastructure
contentBlocks.body:
One of the most powerful and counterintuitive findings in health economics is that investment in primary care produces returns that are comparable to, and in many cases superior to, investment in specialty care infrastructure — not in terms of individual clinical case intensity, but in terms of total population health spending and outcomes. The economic mechanism is straightforward once articulated: primary care reduces the incidence of the expensive downstream events — hospitalizations, emergency visits, specialist procedures, complications of uncontrolled chronic disease — that account for the vast majority of total healthcare spending. A study published in Health Affairs in 2024 analyzing Medicare spending patterns across 306 hospital referral regions found that regions with above-median primary care physician supply had 11.2% lower total Medicare spending per beneficiary, 18.4% fewer preventable hospital admissions, and 14.7% lower 30-day readmission rates than regions with below-median primary care supply, after controlling for demographic and health status differences.

The economic return on primary care investment is particularly relevant for value-based care organizations making resource allocation decisions. Under fee-for-service, a hospital has limited financial incentive to invest in expanding primary care capacity in its community — more primary care visits may mean fewer specialist referrals and fewer hospitalizations, which means less hospital revenue. Under a capitated or shared savings VBC model, the same investment in primary care capacity is a direct cost reduction strategy: every diabetic patient who sees their primary care provider quarterly and maintains target HbA1c levels is a patient who is unlikely to generate an $18,000 diabetic complication admission. The VBC payment model converts primary care from a cost center competing with hospital services for capital allocation into a return-generating infrastructure investment — which is the single most important realignment that value-based payment architecture produces.

The ROI data in the table above carries an important caveat: these are population-level averages from mature ACOs that have already built the data infrastructure to identify high-risk patients, target interventions appropriately, and measure outcomes accurately. An organization implementing a care coordinator program without a functioning risk stratification system to identify which patients the coordinator should prioritize will see substantially lower returns — because care management applied uniformly across a population is far less efficient than care management targeted to the patients most likely to have high-cost events in the next 12 months. The technology readiness discussion in Module 4 is therefore directly connected to the economics of VBC investment: organizations that build population health data infrastructure before scaling care management programs generate significantly better returns than those that sequence these investments in reverse order.

Care coordinators assigned to high-risk patients generate the highest absolute savings per dollar invested, but their effectiveness depends entirely on a functioning risk stratification system that identifies which patients are genuinely high-risk, not just high-cost in the prior year.

Post-discharge follow-up programs have the highest ROI ratio of any single intervention (4.6x) because the cost of a 72-hour phone call is minimal relative to the cost of a readmission, and the evidence that timely follow-up reduces readmissions is among the strongest in care management research.

Community health worker integration produces the largest absolute savings per patient ($1,260 net benefit annually) and is the intervention most directly connected to social determinants of health — addressing food insecurity, housing instability, and transportation barriers that drive utilization patterns that clinical care alone cannot change.

Advanced primary care transformation has the highest total annual investment per patient ($580) but also the highest total annual savings ($2,140), making it the most comprehensive single intervention for organizations ready to redesign their primary care delivery model rather than simply add discrete programs to an unchanged clinical workflow.

contentBlocks.heading: Quote
contentBlocks.body: The organizations that are winning in value-based care are not winning because they have better doctors or better patients. They are winning because they have better data, better targeting, and better financial discipline about which interventions they invest in and for which patient populations. VBC is fundamentally an information business with a clinical delivery layer on top. — Mark McClellan, Duke-Margolis Center for Health Policy, JAMA, 2025.

contentBlocks.heading: Module 3 Summary: The Economics of VBC Reward Patience, Infrastructure, and Precision
contentBlocks.body:
The economics of value-based care are not complicated in their logic, but they are frequently misunderstood in their timing and their requirements. Shared savings arrangements reward population cost management, but only after a benchmark has been established and a minimum savings threshold has been crossed. Bundled payments reward episode cost efficiency, but require investment in post-acute care coordination infrastructure that most hospitals have historically not needed. Capitation rewards comprehensive population health management, but requires actuarial sophistication, quality measurement capability, and working capital reserves that are significant organizational commitments. All three model types have in common a multi-year investment horizon that is at odds with annual budget cycles, and a data infrastructure dependency that is at odds with the technology readiness of many rural and safety-net providers.

The economic case for making these investments nonetheless is clear in the mature ACO data: organizations in their fifth year of MSSP participation generate average shared savings payments of $312 per beneficiary at an investment cost of $87 per beneficiary, a 3.6-to-1 return that compounds as the care management infrastructure matures and the organization’s ability to identify and target high-risk patients improves. The organizations that have reached this performance level did not arrive there by treating VBC as a compliance exercise or a contract opportunity. They treated it as a fundamental redesign of how they organize and deliver care, supported by a financial model that explicitly anticipated and planned for the transition period losses that are the unavoidable cost of that redesign. Module 4 examines the technology infrastructure that makes this financial performance possible.

Review your organization’s current VBC contract portfolio and categorize each contract by model type: shared savings (upside only or two-sided), bundled payment, or capitation. For each contract, identify whether you have a financial model projecting per-beneficiary investment cost, expected savings rate, and net financial benefit over a five-year horizon.

Ask your CFO to quantify the annual fee-for-service revenue at risk from your care management programs — the inpatient admissions and emergency visits that your VBC interventions are intended to prevent, translated into net revenue impact. Compare this to your projected shared savings or capitation savings. If the net is negative, verify your model is using a five-year, not a one-year, planning horizon.

Review the ROI data from the care management intervention table in this module and identify which intervention types your organization is currently investing in. For each intervention, assess whether you have a functioning risk stratification system that targets the intervention to high-risk patients rather than applying it uniformly across your attributed population.

Assess your organization’s actuarial reserve capacity for two-sided risk participation. If your unrestricted net assets are below $15 million, upside-only MSSP participation is the appropriate starting point. If your unrestricted net assets exceed $30 million and you have three or more years of MSSP experience, a formal analysis of ENHANCED track or ACO REACH participation is warranted.

contentBlocks.heading: Key Concept
contentBlocks.body: Module 3 Key Takeaway: The economics of value-based care favor organizations that plan in five-year cycles, invest in care management infrastructure before scaling VBC contract volume, and understand the specific financial mechanics of their contract type at the level of the benchmark calculation and the savings distribution formula. VBC is not a revenue strategy for the next fiscal year. It is a business model for the next decade — one that rewards the organizations that build the infrastructure, accept the transition period losses, and stay the course long enough for the compounding returns of mature care management to materialize.

tracks.title: Bundled Payments
tracks.description: How episode-based bundled payments work, the BPCI Advanced program, which conditions are best suited to bundling, and the evidence on bundle outcomes.

lessons.title: Episode-Based Bundled Payments: How They Work
lessons.summary: The mechanics of bundled payments — episode definition, anchor event, spending window, reconciliation — and which clinical conditions have seen the strongest results.

objectives.text: Explain what a bundled payment episode is and how it is defined
Describe the BPCI Advanced program and which conditions it covers
Explain why post-acute care is the primary savings lever in most bundles

contentBlocks.heading: Paying for the whole episode, not each piece
contentBlocks.body:
A bundled payment sets a single price for all care related to a defined episode — for example, a hip replacement plus 90 days of follow-up care. If the hospital and its partners spend less than the bundle price while meeting quality thresholds, they keep the difference. If they overspend, they owe the difference back.

Bundled payments differ from ACOs in scope: ACOs take accountability for all care for a population over a year. Bundles take accountability for one specific episode — a surgery, a hospitalization for heart failure, a chemotherapy course — plus a defined post-acute window.

contentBlocks.heading: Key bundled payment terms

items.title: Anchor event
items.body: The triggering hospitalization or procedure (e.g., total knee arthroplasty) that begins the episode.

items.title: Episode window
items.body: The time period included in the bundle — typically 30, 60, or 90 days post-anchor. All related care during this window falls within the bundle.

items.title: Target price
items.body: The pre-determined spending target for the episode, based on historical spending adjusted for clinical and geographic factors.

items.title: Reconciliation
items.body: At the end of the performance period, CMS compares actual spending to target. The participant repays overspending or receives a share of savings.

contentBlocks.heading: Post-acute care: where the money is
contentBlocks.body: In most bundled payment conditions, post-acute care (skilled nursing facilities, home health, inpatient rehab) accounts for 40–60% of episode costs. The largest savings opportunity is not in the surgery itself but in reducing unnecessarily long SNF stays, shifting patients to lower-cost settings, and preventing readmissions. High-performing bundle participants carefully manage where patients go after discharge.

contentBlocks.heading: BPCI Advanced: the current Medicare bundle program
contentBlocks.body:
Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced (BPCI Advanced) is CMS's current voluntary bundled payment model. Participants — hospitals or physician group practices — take two-sided risk on 32 clinical episode types, including major joint replacement, hip fracture, COPD, and acute myocardial infarction.

Successful participants have typically invested in: dedicated care coordinators who follow patients from hospital to post-acute, preferred SNF networks with data-sharing agreements, and real-time tracking of episode spending.

lessons.title: Bundled Payment Evidence: What the Research Shows
lessons.summary: The evidence on bundled payment performance across conditions — where bundles have saved money, improved quality, and reduced disparities, and where they have failed.

contentBlocks.heading: The strongest evidence: major joint replacement
contentBlocks.body:
The most robust evidence for bundled payment savings comes from major joint replacement (hip and knee arthroplasty). Studies of BPCI and its predecessor programs show consistent savings of 5–10% on total episode costs, primarily through reduced post-acute spending and lower readmission rates.

Successful joint replacement bundle participants share common features: they established preferred post-acute networks with aligned SNFs, implemented discharge criteria that shifted appropriate patients to home health instead of SNF, and hired care navigators who tracked patients through the 90-day window.

contentBlocks.heading: Equity concern: who avoids complex patients?
contentBlocks.body: A persistent equity critique of bundled payments: providers facing episode cost risk have financial incentives to avoid complex, high-cost patients — those with more comorbidities, lower income, or who live in areas with fewer post-acute options. Studies have found evidence of patient selection in cardiac and orthopedic bundles. CMS has tried to address this through risk adjustment, but critics argue it is insufficient.

lessons.title: The Oncology Care Model: VBC in Cancer Care
lessons.summary: CMS's Oncology Care Model (OCM) and its successor Enhancing Oncology Model (EOM) — how episode-based payment has been applied to cancer chemotherapy and the evidence on performance.

objectives.text: Describe the Oncology Care Model's payment structure
Explain the equity concerns specific to VBC in oncology
Summarize what the OCM evidence showed about savings and quality

contentBlocks.heading: Applying episode payment to cancer
contentBlocks.body:
Cancer care is among the most expensive areas of US healthcare — and among the most difficult to apply episode-based payment models to. Treatment courses vary enormously, clinical pathways are rapidly evolving, and drug costs have been exploding.

The Oncology Care Model (OCM, 2016–2022) covered 6-month episodes anchored by chemotherapy initiation. Practices received a $160/month per-beneficiary-per-month payment for care management, plus shared savings or losses against a benchmark. 187 practices participated at peak.

contentBlocks.heading: OCM results: minimal savings, quality improvement
contentBlocks.body: The final OCM evaluation found minimal net savings to Medicare — about 0.2% of episode costs in the best-performing cohort. However, quality improvements were meaningful: participating practices showed higher hospice use, fewer ED visits, and better symptom documentation. The successor Enhancing Oncology Model (EOM, 2023–) focuses on a smaller set of high-cost cancers with a modified payment approach.

contentBlocks.heading: Equity in oncology VBC

items.title: Patient selection risk
items.body: Practices may avoid enrolling complex patients with more comorbidities or limited social support who are more likely to generate losses.

items.title: Geography
items.body: Rural practices lack post-acute partners and palliative care resources that urban practices can leverage to control episode costs.

items.title: Racial disparities
items.body: Black cancer patients have historically received less aggressive treatment. VBP models that reward cost reduction must ensure they don't reinforce undertreatment.

items.title: Drug costs
items.body: Cancer drug prices have risen 10–15% annually. Episode benchmarks can be overwhelmed by new drug approvals mid-performance period.

questions.explanation: The OCM showed minimal net savings to Medicare (about 0.2% of episode costs) but meaningful quality improvements — higher hospice use, fewer ED visits.

lessons.title: HEDIS, eCQMs & the Quality Measurement Ecosystem
lessons.summary: The landscape of quality measures — who creates them, how they are reported, what HEDIS and eCQMs are, and the ongoing debate about measure burden and meaningful measurement.

objectives.text: Distinguish between HEDIS measures and eCQMs and how each is collected
Identify the major measure stewards and their roles

contentBlocks.heading: The measurement ecosystem
contentBlocks.body: Healthcare quality measurement involves multiple organizations creating, endorsing, and reporting measures — often with different methodologies, data sources, and populations. The result is a measurement ecosystem that is rich in data but fragmented in practice.

contentBlocks.heading: Key players in quality measurement

items.title: NCQA
items.body: National Committee for Quality Assurance. Creates HEDIS measures — the most widely used quality measures in the US, reported by health plans for their populations.

items.title: CMS
items.body: Operates the eCQM (electronic clinical quality measure) program, the Hospital Compare reporting system, and ties measures to payment in VBC programs.

items.title: NQF
items.body: National Quality Forum. Endorses measures through a consensus process — NQF endorsement is required for many federal quality programs.

items.title: Specialty societies
items.body: ACC, ACS, AHA and others create specialty-specific registry measures that complement HEDIS and eCQMs for cardiology, oncology, etc.

contentBlocks.heading: HEDIS vs. eCQMs
Measure burden: the 15-minute visit problem
contentBlocks.body: Physicians now spend an estimated 15+ hours per week on documentation and reporting requirements. Studies show that every patient visit generates 2+ hours of EHR time. CMS has acknowledged the problem and has been actively sunsetting low-value measures, aligning measure sets across programs, and investing in digital quality measure infrastructure to reduce manual reporting burden.

questions.question: HEDIS measures are primarily reported by which type of organization?
questions.explanation: HEDIS measures are reported by health plans (not individual providers) based on claims and medical records for their enrolled populations.

options.text: Individual physicians, who submit data directly to NCQA
Health plans, based on claims and medical records for their enrolled populations
Hospitals, through their EHR systems
State health departments, based on public health surveillance data

lessons.title: Patient-Reported Outcomes: Measuring What Patients Care About
lessons.summary: The shift from clinician-measured to patient-reported outcomes (PROs), the PROMIS framework, CMS's use of PROs in VBC programs, and the implementation challenges.

objectives.text: Explain what patient-reported outcomes are and why they matter for quality measurement
Describe the PROMIS measurement framework and its advantages
Identify how CMS is incorporating PROs into value-based care programs

contentBlocks.heading: What the patient experiences matters most
contentBlocks.body:
Most quality measures capture process (did we do the recommended thing?) or intermediate outcome (did the patient's A1c improve?). Rarely do they ask: how does the patient feel? Can they do what they want to do? Is their pain tolerable? These patient-reported outcomes (PROs) capture the dimensions of health that patients care about most — and that don't appear in clinical records.

PROs are collected via validated questionnaires asking patients directly about their symptoms, function, and quality of life. They are distinct from satisfaction surveys (CAHPS) — PROs measure health states, not opinions about care.

contentBlocks.heading: Key PRO frameworks

items.title: PROMIS
items.body: Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System. NIH-funded standardized measures across physical function, fatigue, pain, depression, anxiety, social functioning. Calibrated by item response theory — adaptive short-form versions available.

items.title: KOOS/HOOS
items.body: Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score / Hip disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score. Condition-specific PROs used in orthopedic bundles and joint replacement episodes.

items.title: ICHOM sets
items.body: International Consortium for Health Outcomes Measurement. Condition-specific standard outcome sets developed with patient input — used globally to enable comparison across health systems.

contentBlocks.heading: CMS's move toward PROs
contentBlocks.body: CMS has begun incorporating PROs into several programs: joint replacement bundles require functional outcome reporting, MIPS has PRO-based quality measures, and the ACO PC Flex model incorporates patient experience measures. The challenge: collecting PROs at scale requires patient portal infrastructure, engagement, and support for patients with limited digital access.

questions.question: What distinguishes patient-reported outcomes (PROs) from patient satisfaction surveys like CAHPS?
questions.explanation: PROs measure health states — symptoms, function, quality of life as experienced by the patient. CAHPS measures patient experience and satisfaction with care delivery, not health status.
