lessons.title: From Volume to Value at the Bedside: How Value-Based Care Transforms Clinical Practice
lessons.summary: Value-based care is not just a billing change — it reshapes what happens in every exam room, every hospital ward, and every care team huddle. This module explores how the shift from fee-for-service to value changes clinical workflows, team structures, quality measurement, population health management, and care coordination. If you practice, manage, or support clinical care in any setting, this module explains why the ground is shifting beneath your feet — and what to do about it.

objectives.text: Explain how fee-for-service versus value-based payment creates different clinical incentives and workflows
Identify the four major domains of quality measurement used in VBC contracts
Define population health management and describe how it works in a primary care setting
Explain what care coordination involves and why it reduces both cost and harm
Describe evidence-based interventions that reduce preventable hospitalizations and readmissions
Identify Vermont-specific clinical programs that operationalize value-based care

contentBlocks.body:
Picture a primary care physician seeing 24 patients in a day. Under fee-for-service, she is rewarded for each visit, each test ordered, each referral made. Under value-based care, she is rewarded for something harder to measure but far more important: whether her patients are actually healthier. That shift in incentives changes everything that happens in the exam room.

This module is about the clinical side of the VBC transformation. It is not abstract. The shift shows up in care team huddles, in how discharge plans are written, in how nurses manage phone calls with patients just released from the hospital, and in how a physician spends the last five minutes of every appointment. Understanding these changes is essential for anyone who works in, manages, or influences clinical care.

contentBlocks.heading: How Payment Models Shape Clinical Decisions
contentBlocks.body:
Clinicians do not consciously think 'I am going to order this test because I will get paid for it.' But payment systems create incentive structures that shape behavior in powerful ways. Under fee-for-service, a busy practice survives by filling the schedule. Under value-based care, a practice is rewarded for keeping patients healthy enough that they do not need to come back as often.

These differences are not just philosophical. They have real operational consequences. A practice moving to value-based contracts must restructure its workflows, hire different staff — care coordinators, community health workers, data analysts — and invest in systems that identify which patients are at risk before they land in the emergency room.

contentBlocks.heading: Quality Measures: How Clinical Performance Is Evaluated
contentBlocks.body: In value-based care, clinicians and practices are evaluated on a structured set of quality measures — standardized metrics that assess whether patients are receiving evidence-based care and achieving good outcomes. These come from several sources: the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, the National Committee for Quality Assurance, and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality.

contentBlocks.heading: Key Concept
contentBlocks.body: Quality Measure: A standardized, evidence-based metric used to assess whether patients receive recommended care. Examples: the percentage of diabetic patients with HbA1c under 8.0%, the percentage of patients with hypertension whose blood pressure is controlled, or the percentage of eligible patients who received a colorectal cancer screening.

There are hundreds of quality measures in use across the US healthcare system. For primary care practices in most VBC contracts, a core set of 10 to 20 measures typically drives the bulk of performance-based bonuses or penalties. The most important fall into four categories.

The most sophisticated VBC programs now move beyond process measures — did we do the right thing? — toward outcome measures: did the patient get better? Vermont's All-Payer Model tracks outcomes like population-level diabetes prevalence trends and preventable hospitalization rates, not just whether a doctor ordered a hemoglobin A1c test.

contentBlocks.heading: Population Health Management: Responsibility Beyond the Appointment
contentBlocks.body:
One of the most fundamental shifts in value-based care is moving from patient-by-patient thinking to population-level thinking. Under fee-for-service, a physician's responsibility begins when a patient walks through the door and ends when they leave. Under VBC, a care team is responsible for the health of an entire attributed patient panel — including the people who are not coming in.

Population health management requires three things fee-for-service practices rarely had: data, staff, and proactive processes. The data comes from electronic health records and claims. The staff — care managers or medical assistants in expanded roles — conduct outreach to patients who need follow-up. The processes include monthly panel reviews, risk stratification algorithms, and care gap closure protocols.

Risk stratification is the engine of population health management. Practices use algorithms — built into EHR systems or analytics platforms — to sort patients into tiers based on their likelihood of a high-cost clinical event in the next 6 to 12 months. High-risk patients get intensive care management: regular check-ins, home visits, medication reconciliation. Low-risk patients get preventive outreach: reminders for annual wellness visits and screenings.

contentBlocks.heading: Care Coordination: The Connective Tissue of Value-Based Care
contentBlocks.body: The US healthcare system was built around specialization. Cardiologists manage hearts. Endocrinologists manage diabetes. Orthopedic surgeons manage joints. This works extraordinarily well for complex procedures and rare conditions. It works catastrophically poorly for the average Medicare patient with five chronic conditions who sees seven different specialists — none of whom talk to each other.

contentBlocks.heading: Key Concept
contentBlocks.body: Care Coordination: The deliberate organization of patient care activities and the sharing of information among all participants to achieve safer, more effective care. It includes communication between providers, follow-up after transitions, medication reconciliation, and ensuring patients understand their care plan.

Poor care coordination is expensive and dangerous. When a cardiologist adds a new medication and does not know the patient's nephrologist recently changed a kidney medication, the combination can cause serious harm. When a hospital discharges a patient with instructions to 'schedule a follow-up within a week' but does not help make that appointment, the patient often does not go — and ends up back in the ER within 30 days.

Value-based care fixes this by making coordination an explicit responsibility with a named owner. The care coordinator — often a registered nurse, social worker, or medical assistant in an extended role — serves as the connective tissue between providers, between hospital and home, and between patient and care plan. Their job is to make sure nothing falls through the cracks.

contentBlocks.heading: Reducing Preventable Hospitalizations and Readmissions
contentBlocks.body: Hospitalizations are the single largest driver of healthcare costs. A single inpatient stay for a Medicare patient costs, on average, more than $13,000. Many of those hospitalizations are for conditions that, if managed properly in an outpatient setting, should never have required a hospital bed. These are called ambulatory care-sensitive conditions — uncontrolled diabetes, COPD exacerbations, congestive heart failure, urinary tract infections.

contentBlocks.heading: Note
contentBlocks.body: Ambulatory Care-Sensitive Conditions (ACSCs): Medical conditions for which timely and appropriate outpatient care can prevent hospitalization. They include asthma, COPD, congestive heart failure, diabetes complications, and hypertension. High ACSC hospitalization rates signal that primary care access or quality is failing.

Value-based care contracts explicitly target ACSC hospitalization rates as a key performance indicator. A practice with a high ACSC rate is leaving money on the table — and more importantly, leaving patients in harm's way. Hospitalizations carry real clinical risk: hospital-acquired infections, medication errors, delirium in elderly patients, and the deconditioning from days of bed rest.

Readmissions are a related but distinct problem. A readmission occurs when a patient returns to the hospital within 30 days of discharge. The national Medicare readmission rate hovers around 15 to 20 percent. CMS began financially penalizing hospitals for excess readmissions in 2013 under the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program. Since then, rates have declined — but remain stubbornly high.

contentBlocks.heading: The New Clinical Team: Roles That Value-Based Care Built
contentBlocks.body:
Value-based care has not replaced physicians. But it has radically expanded the clinical team around them. In a well-functioning VBC practice, the physician is the expert clinician and diagnostic mind — supported by a team that handles much of what was once shoved into a 15-minute visit or never done at all.

Advanced Practice Providers — nurse practitioners and physician assistants — play an expanded role in VBC models, often managing the bulk of stable chronic disease visits and wellness exams while physicians focus on complex diagnostic cases. This is team-based care: the right person, for the right patient, at the right time.

contentBlocks.heading: Vermont Clinical Programs: Value-Based Care in Action
contentBlocks.body:
Vermont is not just talking about value-based clinical care — it has been running the experiment for over a decade. The Blueprint for Health, launched in 2006, was one of the first statewide primary care transformation programs in the country. Every participating practice has undergone a formal practice transformation process: team-based care, patient registries, care coordination, and quality measurement.

Vermont's All-Payer Model, which launched in 2017 and runs through 2029, takes this further. OneCare Vermont — the state's accountable care organization — holds a global budget covering roughly a third of Vermont residents. Practices within OneCare are responsible for the total cost of care for their attributed population. Every preventable hospitalization and readmission is a financial signal that something in the clinical model needs to change.

contentBlocks.heading: The Clinical Case for Value-Based Care
contentBlocks.body:
For many clinicians, the shift to value-based care feels like an administrative imposition — more metrics to track, more documentation requirements, more meetings. That is a legitimate concern, and it reflects real transition pain. But the underlying logic of VBC aligns more closely with why most clinicians entered medicine than fee-for-service ever did.

Fee-for-service rewarded doing more. It paid well for procedures and poorly for conversations, care coordination, and prevention. It created a system where a physician who spent 45 minutes with a complex elderly patient on 12 medications was paid the same as a physician who spent 10 minutes. It created burnout among clinicians who wanted to practice relationship-based medicine but were trapped on a volume treadmill.

contentBlocks.heading: Note
contentBlocks.body: Physician burnout is at crisis levels: 63% of physicians report burnout symptoms, with administrative burden and loss of clinical autonomy cited as primary drivers. VBC, done well, can restore what drew clinicians to medicine: time with patients, team support, and a payment system that rewards doing what is actually right for the patient. Source: AMA National Burnout Survey, 2025.

tracks.title: Risk Adjustment
tracks.description: Why risk adjustment is essential to fair value-based payment, how HCC-based risk scoring works, and the gaming and equity problems with current models.

lessons.title: Risk Adjustment & HCC Scores: Leveling the Playing Field
lessons.summary: Why risk adjustment is necessary for fair VBC payment, how Hierarchical Condition Categories (HCCs) work, how risk scores affect revenue, and the upcoding controversy.

objectives.text: Explain why risk adjustment is necessary for fair comparison in VBC
Describe how HCC-based risk scores are calculated
Explain the upcoding problem and its consequences for the program

contentBlocks.heading: The selection problem
contentBlocks.body:
Without risk adjustment, value-based payment rewards providers who serve healthy patients and penalizes those who serve the sickest. A primary care practice that attracts many elderly patients with multiple chronic conditions will spend more on their care — not because they're inefficient, but because their patients need more care.

Risk adjustment solves this by adjusting payment targets (and quality measure comparisons) based on predicted spending for each patient's health status. A provider with sicker patients gets a higher benchmark; one with healthier patients gets a lower one.

contentBlocks.heading: HCC risk scores: how they're built
contentBlocks.body:
CMS uses a Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) model to calculate each Medicare beneficiary's risk score (Risk Adjustment Factor, or RAF). The model works like this:

1. Claims are submitted by providers with ICD-10 diagnosis codes
2. Diagnoses map to one of 86 HCC categories (e.g., HCC 19 = diabetes without complications, HCC 18 = diabetes with chronic complications)
3. Each HCC has a coefficient representing its contribution to predicted spending
4. The sum of all a patient's HCC coefficients plus demographic factors = their RAF score
5. RAF 1.0 = average cost; RAF 2.0 = twice average cost

Organizations in risk-based contracts are paid based on their population's average RAF — higher RAF populations receive higher per-member-per-month payments.

contentBlocks.heading: The upcoding problem
contentBlocks.body: Because RAF scores translate directly to revenue, there are strong financial incentives to ensure all diagnoses are captured — and, in some cases, to document conditions that may be questionable. OIG and DOJ investigations have found that Medicare Advantage plans (which also use HCC-based risk adjustment) have overstated member acuity by billions of dollars annually through systematic upcoding. CMS has responded with stricter audits and risk score adjustments.

lessons.title: Social Risk in Risk Adjustment: Should We Adjust for Poverty?
lessons.summary: The contested question of whether to include social risk factors in clinical quality risk adjustment — arguments on both sides and the NASEM recommendations.

objectives.text: Explain the argument for including social risk factors in quality measure risk adjustment
Explain the argument against adjusting for social risk
Summarize the NASEM recommendations on social risk adjustment

contentBlocks.heading: The core tension
contentBlocks.body:
Risk adjustment corrects for clinical complexity so that providers caring for sicker patients aren't unfairly penalized on quality or cost measures. The question: should social risk factors — poverty, housing instability, limited English proficiency — be adjusted for in the same way?

Providers argue yes: safety-net hospitals and practices caring for high-poverty populations face structural barriers to quality outcomes that have nothing to do with the quality of their care. Adjusting for social risk levels the playing field.

Equity advocates argue no: adjusting for poverty sets lower quality expectations for poor patients — essentially accepting worse care for the disadvantaged. The goal should be to close gaps, not to hide them.

contentBlocks.heading: Arguments for and against social risk adjustment

rows.label: Fairness
rows.left: Providers caring for high-social-risk patients face barriers beyond their control
rows.right: Adjustment accepts lower quality expectations for poor patients

rows.label: Access
rows.left: Without adjustment, providers may avoid high-risk populations to protect scores
rows.right: Incentives to improve social determinants may be reduced if gaps are adjusted away

rows.label: Accountability
rows.left: Penalizing safety-net providers unfairly may close them, harming access further
rows.right: Accountability requires measuring actual outcomes without excusing poor performance

contentBlocks.heading: NASEM's 2017 recommendation: stratify, don't adjust
contentBlocks.body: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) recommended stratifying quality measure results by social risk — reporting performance separately for high and low social risk patients — rather than adjusting measures to reduce apparent gaps. This preserves accountability for all providers while revealing where disparities exist. CMS has moved toward this approach.

questions.question: What did NASEM recommend for handling social risk in quality measurement?
questions.explanation: NASEM recommended stratifying quality measure results by social risk — reporting separately for high and low social risk patients — rather than adjusting measures to hide gaps.

options.text: Adjust all quality measures for social risk factors in addition to clinical risk
Stratify results by social risk to reveal disparities while preserving accountability
Exclude safety-net providers from quality measurement programs entirely
Give safety-net providers bonus payments without quality measurement requirements

tracks.title: Star Ratings & Consumer Transparency
tracks.description: How CMS Star Ratings work for Medicare Advantage and Part D plans, what's in the 5-star formula, and how Star Ratings drive plan behavior and consumer choice.

lessons.title: Medicare Advantage Star Ratings: Formula, Stakes & Strategy
lessons.summary: How CMS calculates 1-5 star ratings for Medicare Advantage plans, what the financial stakes are, and how plans manage their star strategy.

objectives.text: Explain the 5-star rating formula and its major domains
Describe the financial consequences of star rating levels for MA plans
Identify the measures with the highest weight and strategic importance

contentBlocks.heading: Stars as a market signal and a financial lever
contentBlocks.body:
CMS rates every Medicare Advantage and Part D plan on a 1–5 star scale, published annually on Medicare.gov. Stars serve two purposes: consumer transparency (beneficiaries can compare plans) and financial incentives (CMS pays quality bonuses to plans rated 4 stars or above).

The stakes are enormous. A plan earning 4+ stars receives a 5% bonus on its base payment rate — worth hundreds of millions of dollars annually for large plans. Plans below 3 stars for three consecutive years can be terminated from Medicare Advantage.

contentBlocks.heading: The 5 star domains

items.title: Staying healthy
items.body: Preventive screenings and vaccines — mammograms, colorectal cancer screening, flu vaccines, annual wellness visits.

items.title: Managing chronic conditions
items.body: HEDIS measures for diabetes, hypertension, cholesterol, COPD, and mental health medication adherence.

items.title: Plan responsiveness
items.body: CAHPS member experience measures — getting needed care, getting care quickly, rating of health care, customer service.

items.title: Member complaints & appeals
items.body: Complaint rates, appeals upheld, call center performance metrics.

items.title: Health plan administration
items.body: Compliance with CMS rules, pricing accuracy, and formulary compliance for Part D.

contentBlocks.heading: Highest-weight measures: where plans focus
contentBlocks.body: CMS assigns different weights to different measures — some count 3x, 4x, or 5x in the final calculation. The highest-weight measures include medication adherence for chronic conditions, care for older adults, and care transitions. Plans invest most heavily in improving these measures because the return on a star improvement is highest.

contentBlocks.hint: Interview a Medicare Advantage quality director about which star measures are hardest to move, what interventions have worked, and how the star program has changed plan behavior. Recommended: 8–10 minutes.

questions.explanation: Plans rated 4+ stars receive a 5% quality bonus on their base payment rate from CMS — a significant financial incentive that drives plan investment in quality improvement.

lessons.title: Star Ratings & Equity: The Low-Income Subsidy Problem
lessons.summary: Why Medicare Advantage plans serving high proportions of low-income and dual eligible members consistently score lower on Star Ratings — and what CMS is doing about it.

objectives.text: Explain why plans serving LIS/dual eligible populations score lower on Star Ratings
Describe the criticism that Stars penalizes safety-net MA plans
Explain how the Health Equity Index attempts to address this

contentBlocks.heading: Stars and the equity penalty
contentBlocks.body:
Research consistently shows that Medicare Advantage plans serving higher proportions of Low-Income Subsidy (LIS) beneficiaries and dual eligibles score lower on Star Ratings — even after controlling for plan characteristics. This creates a troubling dynamic: plans that choose to serve the most vulnerable populations are financially penalized through lower star ratings and loss of the 5% quality bonus.

Analyses by MedPAC, CMS, and academic researchers find that 20–30% of the variance in star ratings is explained by the socioeconomic composition of a plan's enrollment — not by actual quality of care delivered.

contentBlocks.heading: The Health Equity Index: CMS's response
contentBlocks.body: Starting with 2027 Star Ratings, CMS is implementing the Health Equity Index (HEI) — a reward measure that gives plans additional credit for achieving better quality outcomes for their LIS/dual eligible and/or disability members. Plans with smaller quality gaps between vulnerable and non-vulnerable members earn HEI credit. This inverts the old incentive: rather than penalizing plans for serving difficult populations, HEI rewards plans that actually close gaps within those populations.

questions.question: What is the equity concern with the current Medicare Advantage Star Ratings system?
questions.explanation: Plans serving high proportions of low-income and dual eligible members consistently score lower on Stars, losing the quality bonus — which may discourage plans from serving these populations.

lessons.title: Who Gets Left Behind: Health Equity, Social Determinants, and Building a VBC System That Works for Everyone
lessons.summary: Value-based care was designed, in part, as a health equity intervention — rewarding good outcomes rather than high volume should help the patients who need the most help. But the research tells a more complicated story. This module examines where VBC has advanced health equity, where it has undermined it, and what specific design choices — in risk adjustment, community health worker programs, panel selection, and rural policy — are required to build a VBC system that actually works for everyone.

objectives.text: Define health disparities and social determinants of health using current data
Explain three structural equity flaws in how most VBC programs are currently designed
Describe how SDOH risk adjustment works and why the current CMS approach is considered insufficient
Explain the evidence base for community health workers and the reimbursement barriers they face
Identify Vermont-specific equity challenges including rural, refugee, and indigenous populations
Describe what equity-centered VBC design requires beyond good intentions

contentBlocks.body:
In 2019, a landmark study published in the journal Science made a startling discovery. A widely used commercial algorithm — the kind that decides which patients get enrolled in intensive care management programs — was systematically underestimating the health needs of Black patients. Not by a little. The algorithm assigned Black patients the same risk score as white patients who were, on average, significantly healthier. The practical consequence: Black patients were less likely to be identified for the high-intensity care management they needed.

This module is the culmination of the course — and arguably its most important chapter. Value-based care promises to improve health for everyone by aligning incentives with outcomes rather than volume. But a payment reform that perpetuates or amplifies existing health inequities is not a solution. It is a new version of the same problem. Understanding where VBC fails on equity — and how to fix it — is not optional knowledge for healthcare leaders. It is the central challenge of our generation.

contentBlocks.heading: What Health Disparities Actually Look Like
contentBlocks.body: A health disparity is a difference in health outcomes between population groups that is preventable, avoidable, and unjust. It is not just the observation that some groups are sicker than others — it is the recognition that those differences are not random. They reflect systematic disadvantages in access to healthcare, economic stability, education, safe housing, and healthy food.

contentBlocks.heading: Key Concept
contentBlocks.body: Health Disparity: A preventable difference in the burden of disease, injury, violence, or opportunity to achieve optimal health between groups defined by race, ethnicity, income, education, disability, geography, or other social characteristics.

These disparities are not primarily explained by genetic differences or individual health behaviors. The research literature is clear: the most powerful predictors of health outcomes are social and economic — where you live, what you earn, whether your neighborhood has a grocery store, whether you can take a day off work to see a doctor. These are the social determinants of health.

contentBlocks.heading: Social Determinants of Health: The 30 to 55 Percent of Outcomes We Rarely Treat
contentBlocks.body:
Social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age that shape health outcomes. They include: income and wealth, educational attainment, employment quality, food security, housing stability and quality, transportation access, neighborhood safety, and social connectedness. The evidence that SDOH factors account for 30 to 55 percent of health outcome variation — compared to only 10 to 20 percent typically attributed to clinical care — is now firmly established in the research literature.

The most frequently screened SDOH domains in clinical settings are food insecurity, housing instability, transportation barriers, social isolation, interpersonal violence, and low health literacy. Standardized screening tools — including the Accountable Health Communities tool and the PRAPARE instrument — allow clinical teams to systematically identify SDOH needs during routine visits. But screening alone is insufficient. The critical next step — connecting patients to community resources that address those needs — is where most health systems still struggle.

contentBlocks.heading: Three Structural Equity Flaws in Current VBC Design
contentBlocks.body:
Value-based care was intended to be an equity intervention — aligning incentives with population health outcomes should, in theory, help the patients who need the most help. The reality is more complicated. Three structural equity problems have been consistently documented in the VBC research literature. Understanding all three is essential for any leader who wants to build VBC programs that advance rather than undermine health equity.

The panel selection problem is the most empirically documented. A 2024 study in Health Affairs found that ACOs serving the highest quartile of dual-eligible beneficiaries — patients enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid, who face the most complex social and clinical needs — were 2.3 times more likely to exit MSSP within three years than ACOs serving lower proportions of dual-eligible patients. The program's financial structure creates systematic pressure against serving the most vulnerable populations.

contentBlocks.heading: Note
contentBlocks.body: A value-based care model that makes it financially rational to avoid serving the sickest, poorest, and most socially complex patients is not a health equity intervention. It is a health equity obstruction wearing the language of reform. Getting the incentives right requires explicit equity design — not just good intentions layered on top of metrics that were built for a different patient population.

contentBlocks.heading: SDOH Risk Adjustment: Making the Metrics Fair
contentBlocks.body:
The metric design problem — the failure of standard quality metrics to account for social determinants — is the most technically solvable of VBC's equity challenges. SDOH risk adjustment means modifying performance benchmarks to account for the social complexity of the patient population being served, so that providers are compared to peers serving similar populations rather than to the national average.

CMS made its most significant commitment to SDOH risk adjustment in the 2022 MSSP final rule, which introduced a Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment that increases spending benchmarks for ACOs serving high proportions of patients with low-income subsidy status. This acknowledges that high-need populations cost more to manage effectively. However, the 3.5 percent adjustment ceiling is widely considered insufficient by health equity researchers — and it uses low-income subsidy status as an imperfect proxy for the full range of social complexity that drives outcome variation.

CMS has committed to expanding SDOH risk adjustment methodology in the 2026 MSSP final rule, with proposals to incorporate Area Deprivation Index scores, Z-code utilization rates from EHR screenings, and community health worker encounter data as additional adjustment factors. These changes are meaningful but still incomplete. The policy change required to make VBC metrics truly equitable will require sustained advocacy from providers who are experiencing the consequences of inadequate adjustment directly.

contentBlocks.heading: Community Health Workers: The Most Powerful Equity Tool in VBC
contentBlocks.body: Community health workers — frontline public health workers who are typically members of the communities they serve, with lived experience of the social and health challenges those communities face — are emerging as the most powerful equity tool in value-based care. Where clinical care coordinators manage disease processes and care transitions, CHWs address the social and environmental factors that determine whether clinical interventions succeed.

contentBlocks.heading: Key Concept
contentBlocks.body: Community Health Worker (CHW): A frontline public health worker who is a trusted member of and has a close understanding of the community being served. CHWs serve as a bridge between health and social services and the communities they serve, reduce cultural and social barriers to care, and provide health education, advocacy, and social support in community settings. They are NOT case managers or care coordinators — the community trust and cultural competence that makes their work effective must be lived, not credentialed.

What makes CHWs distinctive — and irreplaceable — is trust. In communities that have historically had reason to distrust institutional medicine, a CHW who grew up in the neighborhood, speaks the language, and has navigated the same systems can accomplish what no clinical protocol can. They connect patients to food assistance programs, navigate housing resources, provide transportation to appointments, and serve as advocates within a healthcare system that can feel foreign and hostile to those who most need it.

Despite this evidence base, CHW integration into VBC programs has been slower than warranted, primarily because of reimbursement barriers. Most fee-for-service billing structures do not include a direct reimbursement pathway for CHW services, requiring VBC organizations to fund CHW positions out of shared savings or grants. This creates funding fragility — organizations that cannot sustain CHW positions between shared savings payments cycle through workforce disruption that undermines the relationship continuity that makes CHW programs effective.

CMS has taken meaningful steps to address this. The 2024 Medicaid CHW Coverage Rule created a federal minimum standard requiring all state Medicaid programs to provide reimbursement for defined CHW services by 2026. The AHEAD Model's health equity investment fund provides direct CHW program funding in participating states. Vermont, as an AHEAD participant, has an explicit CHW funding stream tied to the All-Payer Model performance requirements.

contentBlocks.heading: Rural and Geographic Equity: The Invisible Disparity
contentBlocks.body:
Healthcare equity discussions in the United States have historically focused primarily on racial and ethnic disparities — and for important reasons. But a parallel geographic equity crisis receives far less policy attention: the systematic disadvantage faced by rural Americans in healthcare access, provider supply, and health outcomes relative to their urban peers.

Rural Americans are more likely to die from the five leading causes of preventable death — heart disease, cancer, unintentional injury, chronic lower respiratory disease, and stroke. They have fewer physicians per capita, longer travel distances to care, higher rates of uninsurance, and significantly lower rates of receiving recommended preventive services. And they are, as documented in the Technology module, disproportionately outside the VBC system entirely — receiving care under fee-for-service Medicare with its documented incentive failures.

contentBlocks.heading: Vermont's Equity Landscape: Progress and Persistent Gaps
contentBlocks.body:
Vermont's All-Payer Model includes an explicit health equity performance requirement — a condition not present in most VBC programs nationally. The AHEAD Model requires participating states to establish measurable health equity goals and report progress annually. Vermont's current equity focus areas include reducing rural-urban disparities in preventive care rates, improving mental health access in rural counties, and addressing the health needs of Vermont's growing refugee and immigrant populations.

Vermont's refugee and immigrant populations — concentrated primarily in Burlington, Winooski, and Rutland — face compounding health equity challenges: language barriers, cultural differences in health-seeking behavior, immigration status concerns, trauma histories from displacement and persecution, and limited familiarity with a healthcare system very different from those in their countries of origin. Vermont's Blueprint for Health has piloted culturally adapted CHW programs for refugee communities, but coverage remains incomplete.

Vermont's Abenaki and other indigenous communities face health disparities that reflect both geographic isolation and historical trauma with healthcare institutions. The legacy of forced assimilation, medical experimentation, and involuntary sterilization programs has created well-founded distrust of the healthcare system that no appointment reminder or care coordinator can overcome. Rebuilding trust with indigenous communities requires sustained, community-led engagement over years — not program cycles.

contentBlocks.heading: AI Bias in Risk Stratification: Technology as an Equity Threat
contentBlocks.body:
The 2019 Science study described at the opening of this module identified a mechanism that explains the algorithmic underestimation of Black patients' health needs: the algorithm used healthcare costs as a proxy for health need. Black patients historically had lower healthcare costs — not because they were healthier, but because structural barriers had historically limited their access to care. The algorithm encoded a history of discrimination as a measure of health. The practical consequence: Black patients were significantly less likely to be flagged for high-intensity care management programs.

This problem has been replicated for other demographic groups and other algorithm types. As AI-powered risk stratification tools become increasingly central to VBC care management, the equity risk posed by biased training data becomes increasingly urgent. A healthcare organization that deploys an AI risk model without auditing it for demographic performance disparities is potentially using technology to automate discrimination at scale.

contentBlocks.heading: Key Concept
contentBlocks.body: Technology Governance Requirement: Any healthcare organization deploying an AI risk stratification tool in a VBC context has an ethical and, increasingly, a legal obligation to audit the tool for demographic performance disparities before deployment. The audit should examine whether the model's accuracy varies significantly across racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic subgroups. If it does, the organization must select a different model, recalibrate it for its specific population, or supplement algorithmic scores with clinical and social worker judgment for populations where the algorithm performs poorly.

contentBlocks.heading: Building Equity-Centered VBC: What It Actually Takes
contentBlocks.body: Building a VBC program that genuinely advances health equity rather than performing it in marketing materials requires design choices that are sometimes in tension with the financial optimization logic that drives most VBC strategy discussions. Equity-centered VBC design requires accepting lower short-term shared savings in exchange for serving populations whose care management needs are higher. It requires investing in CHW infrastructure before guaranteed funding arrives. It requires choosing quality metrics that are SDOH-adjusted rather than metrics that produce better scores simply because you serve a more advantaged population.

contentBlocks.heading: Course Conclusion: What Value-Based Care Can and Cannot Do
contentBlocks.body:
Across six modules, this course has examined value-based care through every lens that matters: the economic incentive logic that makes it necessary, the policy architecture that makes it operational, the economics that determine whether it saves money, the technology that makes it analytically possible, the clinical model that determines whether it actually improves patient outcomes, and the equity design requirements that determine whether it works for everyone. The honest conclusion is nuanced but ultimately optimistic.

Value-based care, when designed well, implemented with adequate infrastructure, and evaluated with appropriate equity metrics, produces meaningfully better clinical outcomes than fee-for-service at lower total cost. The fee-for-service system that currently dominates American healthcare is producing the worst outcomes per dollar of any wealthy nation on earth. The most credible available alternative — paying for health rather than for activity — is demonstrably capable of doing better.

What value-based care cannot do, on its own, is eliminate the social determinants of health that account for 30 to 55 percent of outcome variation. It cannot provide affordable housing, food security, safe neighborhoods, or living wages — the most powerful health interventions available at the population level. These are not arguments against value-based care. They are arguments for building it with sufficient ambition, equity intentionality, and long-term commitment to match the scale of the problem it is trying to solve.

contentBlocks.heading: Note
contentBlocks.body: Vermont's AHEAD Model participation is the most ambitious attempt in state history to align payment incentives, equity goals, and clinical infrastructure toward a single measurable objective: a healthier population at sustainable cost. Whether it succeeds will depend on the willingness of providers, payers, policymakers, and community organizations to make the hard design choices that equity-centered VBC requires.

tracks.title: The Future of Value-Based Care
tracks.description: Where value-based care is heading: primary care first models, total cost of care at scale, VBC in Medicaid, and the unresolved tensions in the field.

lessons.title: Where VBC Is Heading: Primary Care, Equity & Scale
lessons.summary: The push toward primary care-centric total cost of care models, the challenge of embedding equity into VBC design, and honest assessment of what VBC has and hasn't solved.

objectives.text: Describe the AHEAD model and its significance for multi-payer VBC
Explain how VBC models can be designed to advance or inadvertently undermine equity
Articulate the honest limitations of VBC after 15 years of experimentation

contentBlocks.heading: The primary care investment deficit
contentBlocks.body: Despite 15 years of VBC, the US still underinvests in primary care relative to specialty care. Primary care receives approximately 5–7% of total health spending despite managing the majority of patient contacts. VBC models that pay for total cost of care have shown the most promise when they substantially increase primary care investment — higher per-member payments for care management, behavioral health integration, and extended access.

contentBlocks.heading: Emerging directions in VBC

items.title: AHEAD Model
items.body: CMS's State All Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development (AHEAD) model. Vermont is a participant. Aligns Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial payers around shared total cost of care targets at the state level.

items.title: Equity in VBC
items.body: New CMS requirements for ACOs and MA plans to stratify quality data by race, ethnicity, and social risk — and to develop equity plans to close gaps.

items.title: Advanced Primary Care
items.body: CMS Primary Care First (PCF) and similar models that dramatically increase primary care revenue in exchange for total cost of care accountability.

items.title: Behavioral health integration

contentBlocks.heading: What VBC has not solved
contentBlocks.body: After 15+ years of experimentation: VBC has not bent the cost curve at the population level. National health spending continues to grow faster than GDP. VBC has produced real but modest savings in specific programs. The field has learned that payment reform alone — without workforce transformation, social determinants investment, and technology alignment — is insufficient. The next chapter of VBC will need to address these structural gaps.

lessons.title: Global Budgets for Hospitals: Maryland & Beyond
lessons.summary: How global hospital budgets set annual spending targets that decouple hospital revenue from volume — the Maryland Model, Vermont, and the evidence on cost and quality.

contentBlocks.heading: The hospital volume problem
contentBlocks.body:
In fee-for-service, hospitals earn revenue when patients are admitted. They lose revenue when patients avoid hospitalization — through better primary care, prevention, or care management. Global budgets fundamentally change this: a hospital receives a fixed annual budget regardless of how many patients it admits. If it can keep patients healthy and out of the hospital, it keeps the budget. If volume rises above target, it must absorb the additional cost.

This is the most complete form of hospital payment reform — aligning hospital financial incentives with population health for the first time.

contentBlocks.heading: Maryland: the only all-payer global budget state
contentBlocks.body:
Maryland has had a unique hospital payment system since 1977. The Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC) sets hospital rates for all payers — Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial — under a federal waiver. In 2014, Maryland entered the Total Cost of Care Model, adding a population-level global budget for Medicare spending across all care settings.

Results after 5 years: Maryland hospitals generated $1.2B in Medicare savings, achieved lower per-capita cost growth than national trends, and showed quality improvements — particularly in preventable hospitalizations and readmissions. Vermont's AHEAD model, which Vermont entered in 2024, is modeled partly on Maryland's approach.
