lessons.title: Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 2: The Policy Pillar — Laws, Rules, and the Regulatory Architecture That Makes (or Breaks) Value-Based Care
lessons.summary: Module 2 of the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course examines the federal and state policy architecture that governs value-based care adoption in the United States. Building on Module 1’s conceptual foundation, this module explains in plain language how MACRA, the ACA’s Innovation Center, and state Medicaid waiver programs create the legal and financial scaffolding for VBC models, identifies the regulatory barriers that slow adoption for rural and safety-net providers, and equips learners to read and interpret the policy signals that will shape their organization’s VBC strategy through 2030. No prior policy or legal background is required.

objectives.text: Explain MACRA's two-track physician payment architecture and the financial difference between MIPS and Advanced APM participation.
Describe how the 2020 Stark Law and Anti-Kickback VBC exceptions enable ACO-physician financial arrangements.
Identify the policy signals — RFIs, fee schedule proposed rules, model termination notices — that indicate future VBC direction.
Compare state Medicaid VBC adoption using Section 1115 and 1915 waiver frameworks.
Summarize the AHEAD Model's all-payer structure and explain why it is architecturally different from single-payer VBC models.

contentBlocks.body: Imagine you want to start a new kind of restaurant — one that charges customers a flat monthly fee to eat as many healthy meals as they need, rather than charging per dish. The idea makes sense nutritionally and economically. But before you open, you discover that local zoning laws require all food establishments to post per-item prices. The health department’s inspection checklist was designed for traditional menus. Your liquor license application has no category for subscription dining. None of these rules were written to block your idea — they were simply written when your idea did not exist. This is precisely the situation that value-based care innovators face in the American healthcare regulatory environment. The laws, billing codes, anti-kickback rules, and licensure frameworks that govern U.S. healthcare were almost entirely written for a fee-for-service world. Navigating, modifying, and sometimes working around them is not a bureaucratic inconvenience for VBC implementation — it is one of its defining challenges.

contentBlocks.heading: Why Policy Is a Pillar, Not Just a Background Condition
contentBlocks.body:
Healthcare is one of the most heavily regulated industries in the United States, and for good reason: the decisions made in healthcare settings involve life and death, profound information asymmetry between providers and patients, and the expenditure of trillions of dollars of public funds. The regulatory architecture that governs healthcare payment — Medicare and Medicaid rules, anti-kickback statutes, the Stark Law governing physician self-referral, state insurance laws, and HIPAA privacy regulations — was built incrementally over six decades, each layer added in response to a specific problem or abuse. The result is a regulatory environment of extraordinary complexity that can simultaneously protect patients and obstruct innovation, often in the same rule. For value-based care specifically, the policy environment matters in three distinct ways: it determines which VBC models are legally permissible, it shapes the financial terms under which VBC contracts can operate, and it establishes the data sharing authorities that VBC’s information infrastructure depends upon.

The good news for learners approaching this material is that you do not need to become a healthcare attorney to understand the policy landscape for VBC. What you do need is a working knowledge of four things: the major federal legislation that authorized and funds VBC programs, the agency — CMS and its Innovation Center — that designs and operates most federal VBC models, the specific legal waivers that allow VBC arrangements to operate outside standard fee-for-service rules, and the state-level Medicaid policy environment that governs VBC adoption for the Medicaid population, which represents 22% of all U.S. healthcare spending and the majority of payer mix for rural and safety-net hospitals. This module covers all four in sequence, with enough practical depth that you can apply the concepts to your organization’s specific situation.

contentBlocks.heading: The ACA’s Innovation Center: The Engine of U.S. VBC Development
contentBlocks.body:
The Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation, universally known as CMMI, was established by Section 3021 of the Affordable Care Act in 2010 with a mandatory appropriation of $10 billion over ten years and a statutory mission to test, evaluate, and scale new payment and delivery models that reduce spending while preserving or improving quality. CMMI’s legal authority is significant: it can implement new payment models for Medicare and Medicaid without going through the standard notice-and-comment rulemaking process that governs most federal regulation, as long as the model operates within specific statutory parameters and is evaluated by CMS’s Office of the Actuary. This streamlined authority was deliberately designed to allow rapid policy experimentation — the legislative drafters recognized that VBC model design requires iteration and learning, and that subjecting every model modification to a 12-month rulemaking cycle would make meaningful innovation impossible.

Since 2011, CMMI has launched more than 50 distinct payment model pilots across Medicare and Medicaid, covering primary care transformation, specialty care bundling, accountable care organizations, direct contracting, and state-level all-payer models. The budget allocated per model varies enormously — from small demonstration projects covering a few thousand beneficiaries to large-scale national programs like the Medicare Shared Savings Program, which enrolled 11.2 million beneficiaries by 2025. CMMI’s mandate requires it to demonstrate that each model either reduces net Medicare spending, improves quality without increasing spending, or both. Models that fail to meet these thresholds are terminated. As of 2025, CMMI has terminated 14 models for insufficient evidence of savings or quality improvement, a track record that reflects honest evaluation but has also generated criticism from providers who invested substantially in model infrastructure before termination decisions.

contentBlocks.heading: Quote
contentBlocks.body: CMMI’s authority to move faster than the standard rulemaking process is its most valuable feature and its most politically contested one. Every model CMMI launches is a hypothesis about how to organize care better. Some hypotheses are wrong. The question is whether the system is learning fast enough from both successes and failures. — Dr. Rahul Rajkumar, former CMMI Deputy Director, Health Affairs Blog, 2024.

contentBlocks.heading: MACRA: The Law That Made VBC Participation Effectively Mandatory for Physicians
contentBlocks.body:
If CMMI is the engine of federal VBC development, the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act of 2015 — universally known as MACRA — is the law that turned VBC from an optional experiment into the default trajectory for physician payment in Medicare. MACRA was passed with rare bipartisan consensus, repealing the deeply unpopular Sustainable Growth Rate formula that had governed Medicare physician payments since 1997 and replacing it with a two-track system that explicitly links physician payment updates to VBC participation. Understanding MACRA’s structure is essential for any clinical or administrative leader whose organization bills Medicare for physician services, because it directly determines how physicians are paid and how much.

MACRA’s two tracks work as follows. Physicians who remain in traditional fee-for-service Medicare participate in the Merit-based Incentive Payment System, or MIPS, which adjusts their annual Medicare payments up or down by up to 9% based on performance across four categories: quality (45% weight), promoting interoperability (25%), improvement activities (15%), and cost (15%). MIPS is designed as a transitional step — it maintains the fee-for-service base payment structure while adding a performance overlay that rewards quality and penalizes inefficiency. The alternative track, and the one that MACRA’s architects intended as the destination, is participation in an Advanced Alternative Payment Model, or APM, which includes CMS-approved VBC arrangements that meet specific risk and quality criteria. Physicians who generate a sufficient share of their Medicare revenue through APM participation receive a 5% lump-sum bonus payment and are exempt from MIPS reporting requirements — a substantial financial incentive to move toward more advanced VBC structures.

contentBlocks.heading: The MIPS-to-APM Progression: What It Looks Like in Practice
contentBlocks.body: The practical effect of MACRA’s two-track architecture is to create a structured pathway from fee-for-service through MIPS participation toward Advanced APM engagement, with financial incentives escalating at each stage. A solo primary care physician in rural Wyoming who bills Medicare exclusively on a fee-for-service basis is automatically enrolled in MIPS and will receive payment adjustments — upward or downward — based on their quality reporting, EHR utilization, and cost performance. The same physician who joins a CMMI-approved Accountable Care Organization and generates 50% of their Medicare revenue through that ACO qualifies as an Advanced APM participant, receives the 5% bonus, and escapes the MIPS reporting burden. MACRA’s architecture was designed to make this progression financially attractive enough that providers would voluntarily move toward advanced VBC structures over time, without the political controversy of making VBC participation legally mandatory.

contentBlocks.heading: Key Concept
contentBlocks.body: Policy Insight for Practice Leaders: If your organization’s physicians are currently in MIPS and scoring below 75, you are almost certainly paying more in administrative reporting costs than you are receiving in payment bonuses. The CMS data consistently shows that the cost of MIPS compliance for small and independent practices averages $12,800 per physician per year in staff time and technology costs. Joining an ACO or Advanced APM eliminates this burden while generating shared savings upside. The question is not whether to make the move — it is when your organization has the infrastructure to do it responsibly.

contentBlocks.heading: The Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute: The Rules VBC Had to Work Around
contentBlocks.body:
Two of the most significant legal barriers to value-based care adoption are laws that were designed to protect patients from fraud: the Stark Law, which prohibits physician self-referral for designated health services when a financial relationship exists between the physician and the referred entity, and the Federal Anti-Kickback Statute, which prohibits offering or receiving anything of value to induce referrals of federal healthcare program business. Both laws were enacted in the 1980s and 1990s to address genuine abuses in fee-for-service medicine — physicians referring patients to laboratories or imaging centers they owned, and pharmaceutical companies paying physicians to prescribe specific drugs. They are important protections. They are also written in a way that, on their face, makes many value-based care arrangements technically illegal.

Consider a simple VBC arrangement: a hospital wants to share a portion of the savings generated by an ACO with the primary care physicians who successfully manage their attributed patient panels and reduce unnecessary hospitalizations. Under a strict reading of the Anti-Kickback Statute, this payment could be characterized as remuneration to physicians for reducing referrals to the hospital — which is exactly what the statute was written to prohibit when the financial relationship runs in the other direction. In November 2020, CMS and the Department of Justice’s Office of Inspector General simultaneously published new rules — commonly called the Stark Law and AKS VBC Exceptions — that created explicit regulatory safe harbors for value-based arrangements meeting specific criteria. These exceptions are the legal foundation on which most current VBC contract structures rest, and understanding their existence (if not their full technical detail) is important context for any leader involved in VBC contract negotiation.

contentBlocks.heading: What the 2020 VBC Exceptions Actually Allow
contentBlocks.body: The 2020 Stark Law and AKS VBC exceptions created three tiers of safe harbor protection based on the level of financial risk the arrangement assumes. The first tier, the “care coordination arrangement” exception, covers low-risk VBC arrangements where physicians and hospitals share non-monetary resources — care coordinators, technology platforms, data analytics tools — without direct financial remuneration flowing between them. The second tier covers arrangements where the parties share substantial downside financial risk, defined as the physician group being responsible for a meaningful share of losses if spending targets are not met. The third and most protective tier applies to arrangements where a physician entity is “fully at risk” — accepting capitation-level accountability for a defined patient population. The practical effect of this tiered structure is that more financially protective exceptions are available to VBC arrangements that accept more financial risk — a policy design that explicitly incentivizes providers to move toward more advanced VBC models in exchange for greater legal certainty.

contentBlocks.heading: State Medicaid Policy: Where VBC Gets Complicated Fast
contentBlocks.body:
Medicaid, the joint federal-state health insurance program for low-income Americans, covers 90 million people and represents 22% of all U.S. healthcare spending. For rural and safety-net hospitals, Medicaid is often the dominant payer — in some Critical Access Hospitals, Medicaid accounts for more than 40% of patient volume. Any serious discussion of VBC adoption must therefore grapple with Medicaid policy, and Medicaid policy is, by design, a state-level affair. Under the Social Security Act, the federal government sets minimum Medicaid standards and matches state spending at rates ranging from 50% to 90% depending on state per-capita income — but states have substantial flexibility in how they design their Medicaid programs, including how they pay providers. This flexibility has produced a 50-state patchwork of Medicaid VBC approaches that range from nationally leading to years behind, often with little correlation to state wealth or healthcare system capacity.

States access this flexibility primarily through two mechanisms: Section 1115 waivers, which allow states to use Medicaid funds in ways not otherwise permitted by federal statute in exchange for CMS approval of a formal waiver application and evaluation framework, and Section 1915 waivers, which allow states to require Medicaid beneficiaries to enroll in managed care organizations rather than traditional fee-for-service Medicaid. As of 2025, 41 states operate Medicaid managed care programs covering at least some beneficiary populations, and 24 states have active Section 1115 waivers that include VBC-oriented payment reform components. The remaining states continue to operate primarily fee-for-service Medicaid programs, creating a two-tier national Medicaid environment where the VBC infrastructure, data systems, and provider capabilities in a given state depend heavily on decisions made by state legislatures and Medicaid agencies that most healthcare professionals are only vaguely aware of.

The state variation in Medicaid VBC adoption documented in the table above is not simply a story of some states moving faster than others. It reflects fundamentally different political economies, administrative capacities, and provider infrastructure realities. Massachusetts’ MassHealth ACO Program, which places 78% of Medicaid beneficiaries in global budget arrangements, required a decade of incremental managed care development, a sophisticated state health information exchange, and a robust community health worker infrastructure before global budgets were feasible. Mississippi, which remains 89% fee-for-service Medicaid, faces not just a political environment less favorable to managed care but a provider infrastructure so financially fragile — as examined in the DSH module — that asking rural hospitals to accept downside financial risk before their basic solvency is secured would be policy malpractice. Understanding this context prevents the common mistake of treating state VBC laggards as simply lacking political will, when the more accurate diagnosis is often a missing infrastructure foundation.

contentBlocks.heading: The AHEAD Model: The Boldest Current Federal VBC Policy Experiment
contentBlocks.body:
The CMS All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development Model, known as AHEAD, launched in 2023 and represents the most ambitious federal VBC policy experiment currently active in the United States. AHEAD is fundamentally different from previous CMS models in one critical way: it operates across all payers simultaneously, not just Medicare. In the eight participating states — Maryland, Vermont, Connecticut, Hawaii, Minnesota, New York, Rhode Island, and Washington — CMS is working with state governments and commercial insurers to establish coordinated spending targets that apply to Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance simultaneously. The goal is to eliminate the perverse incentive created by single-payer VBC models, where a provider that successfully reduces costs for its Medicare ACO population may simply shift utilization to its commercially insured population, producing savings for Medicare at the expense of commercial payer spending.

AHEAD’s architecture has three components that build on each other. Hospital Global Budgets establish annual spending targets for inpatient and outpatient hospital care, similar to the model Maryland has operated since 1977 under a waiver from standard Medicare payment rules. Primary Care Investment establishes a per-capita funding floor for primary care services in each participating state, addressing the underfunding of primary care that Module 1 identified as a structural driver of the U.S. spending-outcomes gap. And the Health Equity Plan requires each participating state to establish specific, measurable goals for reducing health outcome disparities across racial, ethnic, geographic, and socioeconomic dimensions, with CMS oversight of progress toward those goals as a condition of continued model participation. AHEAD’s early results will not be statistically meaningful until 2027 at the earliest, but its structural design represents the most coherent attempt yet to address the whole-system payment reform that health economists have argued is necessary for genuine transformation.

contentBlocks.heading: Quote
contentBlocks.body: The AHEAD Model is not a pilot. It is a policy architecture for what the American healthcare payment system could look like at scale — one where no payer is an island, where primary care is funded as infrastructure rather than as a commodity, and where health equity is a contractual obligation rather than an aspiration. Whether it works depends entirely on whether the participating states build the administrative and data infrastructure to make the targets meaningful. — HTR Regulatory Intelligence Assessment, Q1 2026.

contentBlocks.heading: Reading Policy Signals: How to Know What’s Coming Before It Arrives
contentBlocks.body:
One of the most practical skills a healthcare leader can develop is the ability to read federal policy signals early — to understand what CMS, Congress, and state Medicaid agencies are signaling about the future direction of payment policy before new rules take effect. This skill is valuable because VBC model participation requires organizational investment — in data systems, care management staffing, and actuarial capabilities — that takes 18 to 36 months to build. Organizations that wait until a rule is finalized to begin building readiness will always be behind. The following framework identifies the primary signals that healthcare leaders should monitor continuously as leading indicators of VBC policy direction.

CMS Requests for Information (RFIs) are formal public notices in which CMS invites stakeholder comment on a policy concept before publishing a proposed rule. An RFI on a new payment model concept typically precedes a proposed rule by 12–18 months, giving organizations that monitor them a substantial head start on understanding what is coming and beginning internal readiness assessments.

The Annual Physician Fee Schedule Proposed Rule, published every July for the following calendar year, contains the annual MIPS threshold adjustments, quality measure updates, and any modifications to Advanced APM qualifying criteria. Reading the proposed rule summary — not the full document, which runs to thousands of pages — each July is the single most efficient way to stay current on federal physician payment policy.

CMMI Model Termination Notices are official signals that a payment model has not met its statutory savings or quality thresholds. When CMMI terminates a model, it typically publishes evaluation findings that explain why. Reading these findings is often more instructive than reading the original model design documents, because they identify the specific infrastructure gaps, attribution problems, or market conditions that prevented the model from working — lessons directly applicable to understanding what makes other VBC models succeed.

State Medicaid Managed Care Request for Proposals are published by state Medicaid agencies when they are procuring new managed care contracts, typically on three-to-five year cycles. These documents specify the quality metrics, VBC incentive structures, SDOH screening requirements, and health equity goals that Medicaid managed care organizations and their provider networks will be held to. Organizations that serve Medicaid populations should read their state’s current managed care RFP as a direct statement of the performance expectations they will face in the next contract cycle.

contentBlocks.heading: Module 2 Summary: The Policy Environment Is Not Your Enemy — But You Must Understand It
contentBlocks.body:
The policy architecture governing value-based care in the United States is complex, layered, and still evolving — but it is not impenetrable to practitioners willing to invest in understanding its structure. The key institutions are CMS and its Innovation Center, which design and operate most federal VBC models; Congress, which authorizes and funds VBC infrastructure through legislation like MACRA and the ACA; and state Medicaid agencies, which determine how value-based principles are applied to the Medicaid population that drives solvency for most safety-net and rural providers. The key legal frameworks are MACRA’s two-track physician payment architecture, the 2020 Stark Law and Anti-Kickback VBC exceptions, and the Section 1115 and 1915 waiver authorities that give states flexibility to innovate within federal Medicaid rules.

The most important single insight from this module is that policy does not just regulate VBC — it enables it. The shared savings that MSSP ACOs distribute to physicians are legal because of CMMI’s model authority and the AKS safe harbor. The global budgets that Maryland hospitals operate under are legal because of a 47-year-old CMS waiver. The care coordination resources that a hospital shares with its independent physician partners are legally protected because of the 2020 VBC exceptions. Every advanced VBC arrangement you will encounter in your career rests on a specific legal and regulatory foundation. Understanding that foundation — at least at the level of knowing which questions to ask your legal team — is not optional for any leader who wants to move their organization toward value.

Identify your organization’s current MACRA track: are your physicians primarily in MIPS, in an Advanced APM, or in both? If primarily MIPS, what is the organization’s target timeline for APM qualification, and what infrastructure gaps stand between you and that threshold?

Review your state’s current Medicaid managed care contract or RFP. Identify the three quality metrics with the highest incentive weight and assess your organization’s current performance on each. The gap between your current performance and the contract’s quality bonus threshold is a direct measure of revenue at risk.

Determine whether your state is an AHEAD Model participant. If yes, begin engaging your state hospital association and state health department about the hospital global budget timeline and what data your organization will need to submit. If no, monitor CMS for the next AHEAD cohort solicitation, expected in late 2026.

Schedule a conversation with your legal or compliance team specifically about the 2020 Stark Law and Anti-Kickback VBC exceptions. Ask them to identify any current or planned VBC arrangements at your organization that rely on these exceptions, and to confirm that the arrangements are structured to satisfy the applicable safe harbor criteria.

contentBlocks.heading: Key Concept
contentBlocks.body: Module 2 Key Takeaway: The U.S. healthcare policy environment was built for fee-for-service, but it has been systematically modified over the past 15 years to enable value-based care. CMMI’s model authority, MACRA’s APM incentive structure, the 2020 VBC legal exceptions, and state Medicaid waiver programs together constitute a policy architecture that makes advanced VBC legally and financially feasible for most U.S. healthcare organizations. The organizations that understand this architecture and align their strategy to it are the ones that will be best positioned as CMS accelerates its stated goal of having 100% of Medicare beneficiaries in an accountable care relationship by 2030.

lessons.title: Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 4: The Technology Pillar — Data, AI, and the Digital Infrastructure That Makes VBC Work
lessons.summary: Module 4 of the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course examines the technology infrastructure that value-based care requires to function — and what happens when that infrastructure is missing. This module explains, in plain language, what interoperable electronic health records, health information exchange, and AI-powered risk stratification tools actually do in a VBC context, why 34% of rural Critical Access Hospitals remain technology-unready for advanced VBC participation, and how the federal interoperability agenda — including the 21st Century Cures Act, the CMS Interoperability Rule, and the TEFCA framework — is building the data infrastructure that VBC depends upon. By the end of this module, learners will understand the specific technology capabilities that VBC models require, the sequence in which they should be built, and the federal programs that fund them.

objectives.text: Identify the three technology layers VBC requires and explain why each layer depends on the quality of the layer below it.
Describe what the 21st Century Cures Act's FHIR mandate and information blocking prohibition changed in health IT.
Explain how AI risk stratification improves on claims-based models and why demographic bias auditing is ethically required.
Assess an organization's VBC technology readiness using the rural-urban capability gap framework.
Apply the five-phase technology investment roadmap to prioritize VBC infrastructure investment sequentially.

contentBlocks.body: Imagine trying to run a nationwide airline reservation system where every airport kept its flight records on paper, no two airports used the same form, and sharing records between airports required a fax machine and a three-day waiting period. Connecting passengers to flights would be technically possible but operationally chaotic — delays, lost records, missed connections, and dangerous errors would be routine, not exceptional. This is, only slightly exaggerated, the state of health information exchange in the United States as recently as 2019, and in many rural markets as recently as 2024. Value-based care requires something that American healthcare has never had at scale: a reliable, real-time, standards-based system for sharing patient health information across organizational boundaries. Without it, an Accountable Care Organization cannot know that its attributed Medicare patient was admitted to a hospital outside the network last Tuesday. A care coordinator cannot know that a high-risk patient missed their primary care appointment. A risk stratification algorithm cannot identify a patient approaching a high-cost event without complete longitudinal data about their diagnosis history, medication adherence, and recent utilization. Technology is not a nice-to-have for advanced VBC. It is the operating system on which the entire model runs.

contentBlocks.heading: The Three Technology Layers VBC Requires
contentBlocks.body: The technology infrastructure that supports effective value-based care can be understood as three interdependent layers, each building on the one below it. The foundation layer is clinical data capture: the electronic health record system that documents every patient encounter, diagnosis, medication, order, and result in a structured, machine-readable format. The second layer is data integration and exchange: the health information exchange infrastructure that connects EHR systems across organizations so that complete patient data is available regardless of where care was delivered. The third layer is analytics and intelligence: the population health management platforms, risk stratification tools, and increasingly AI-powered predictive models that transform raw clinical data into actionable care management intelligence — identifying which patients are at highest risk of imminent high-cost events, which chronic disease patients are overdue for interventions, and which populations are generating the most preventable utilization. Each layer is necessary but not sufficient. Strong EHR implementation without HIE connectivity produces siloed data. HIE connectivity without analytics produces data that no one has the capacity to act on. Analytics without high-quality underlying data produces predictions that are wrong in ways that are hard to detect until they cause harm.

contentBlocks.heading: Electronic Health Records: The Foundation Layer
contentBlocks.body:
The United States made a massive federal investment in EHR adoption through the HITECH Act of 2009, which appropriated $27 billion in Medicare and Medicaid incentive payments to encourage providers to implement certified EHR systems and demonstrate “meaningful use” — a defined set of capabilities including electronic prescribing, clinical decision support, and patient portal access. By 2021, 88% of hospitals and 78% of office-based physicians had implemented certified EHR systems, a transformation from the 9% hospital adoption rate that existed in 2008. This is one of the most rapid technology adoption curves in the history of any industry, and it created the clinical data foundation that value-based care analytics requires. However, EHR adoption rates mask significant quality variation that is directly relevant to VBC capability. Having a certified EHR does not mean having a fully configured, fully utilized EHR that generates high-quality structured data. Many providers, particularly smaller rural practices and critical access hospitals, implemented EHR systems at the minimum level required to qualify for HITECH incentive payments, resulting in EHR installations that function primarily as billing and documentation tools rather than population health data platforms.

The VBC-relevant EHR capabilities that matter most are not the basic documentation features that HITECH required, but the advanced data quality and interoperability features that turn an EHR from a digital chart room into a population health intelligence system. These include structured problem lists and medication lists that use standardized coding (ICD-10 for diagnoses, RxNorm for medications, SNOMED CT for clinical concepts) rather than free-text notes; care gap reporting that identifies patients overdue for preventive services or chronic disease monitoring; patient panel management tools that allow care coordinators to view their entire assigned patient population sorted by risk level; and FHIR API connectivity that allows the EHR to exchange data with external systems using the standardized data format that the 21st Century Cures Act mandated in 2020. As of 2024, only 54% of Critical Access Hospitals have all four of these capabilities fully implemented and actively used, compared to 79% of urban academic medical centers — a technology readiness gap that directly correlates with rural hospital VBC participation rates.

contentBlocks.heading: The 21st Century Cures Act: The Law That Changed EHR Interoperability Requirements
contentBlocks.body: The 21st Century Cures Act, enacted in December 2016 with its implementing regulations finalized in 2020, made two changes to the EHR landscape that are directly relevant to VBC technology readiness. First, it prohibited “information blocking” — defined as any practice that unreasonably restricts the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information — and established civil monetary penalties of up to $1 million per violation for health IT developers, networks, and exchanges that engage in information blocking. This provision was specifically designed to address a well-documented pattern in which EHR vendors and some health systems restricted data sharing with competitors or external partners, creating artificial data silos that served commercial interests at the expense of care coordination. Second, it mandated that all certified EHR systems implement standardized FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) application programming interfaces by 2022, enabling third-party developers to build population health applications that connect directly to EHR data without requiring custom integrations. The FHIR mandate is the technical foundation of the modern population health analytics market, as it allows risk stratification platforms, care gap tools, and quality reporting systems to access EHR data through a single standardized connection rather than a patchwork of proprietary integrations.

contentBlocks.heading: Quote
contentBlocks.body: The 21st Century Cures Act’s information blocking prohibition changed the competitive dynamics of health IT in a way that CMS’s interoperability rules alone could not have. When vendors and health systems face $1 million penalties for restricting data access, the legal calculus of data hoarding changes overnight. The challenge now is not permission — it is infrastructure. Building the pipes to carry the data that is now legally required to flow is the work of this decade. — Don Rucker, former National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, Health IT Buzz, 2024.

contentBlocks.heading: Health Information Exchange: The Data Sharing Layer
contentBlocks.body:
Health information exchange (HIE) refers to the electronic sharing of patient health information across organizational boundaries — between hospitals, physician practices, laboratories, pharmacies, and post-acute care providers that may use different EHR systems and operate in different ownership structures. For value-based care, HIE is not optional infrastructure. An ACO that cannot receive notifications when its attributed patients are admitted to or discharged from any hospital in its market cannot manage post-discharge follow-up effectively. A care coordinator who cannot see a patient’s complete medication list across all prescribers cannot identify dangerous drug interactions or medication non-adherence. A risk stratification algorithm that only has access to the patient’s encounters at one health system is working from an incomplete and potentially misleading clinical picture. The importance of HIE to VBC has been recognized in federal policy through TEFCA — the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement — which ONC published in January 2022 as the national framework for interoperable health information exchange.

TEFCA establishes a set of technical and legal standards that health information networks must meet to become Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs), and creates a framework under which QHINs are required to share data with each other upon request, effectively creating a nationwide health information exchange network for the first time. As of early 2026, six organizations have been designated as QHINs: eHealth Exchange, Epic Nexus, CommonWell Health Alliance, Kno2, MedAllies, and KONZA National Network. The coverage of these networks is extensive in urban and suburban markets but remains uneven in rural areas, where the combination of fewer participating providers, older EHR systems, and limited broadband infrastructure creates connectivity gaps that directly limit rural ACO and VBC participants’ ability to receive real-time patient data from non-network sources. The FCC’s Healthcare Connect Fund and USDA’s ReConnect Program are the primary federal mechanisms for addressing rural broadband gaps, but as of 2025, 18% of rural hospital locations still lack broadband access meeting the minimum 25 Mbps threshold that reliable EHR connectivity requires.

The capability gap data in the table above represents a structural VBC readiness disparity that policy interventions alone cannot close without significant capital investment. A rural Critical Access Hospital that lacks FHIR R4 API implementation, state HIE connectivity, and a population health platform is not technically capable of the patient data workflows that MSSP ACO participation requires — not because of organizational will or leadership quality, but because the digital infrastructure that enables those workflows has not been built. The federal programs designed to address this gap — including the FCC Healthcare Connect Fund’s $7.1 billion rural broadband commitment, ONC’s Health IT Certification Program, and HRSA’s Rural Health Information Technology funding stream — are necessary but insufficient at their current funding levels to close the rural-urban technology gap within a policy-relevant timeframe.

contentBlocks.heading: AI and Risk Stratification: The Intelligence Layer
contentBlocks.body:
Risk stratification — the process of identifying which patients within a large population are at highest risk of future high-cost health events — is the intelligence function that turns population health data into actionable care management priorities. In a VBC model managing 10,000 attributed patients, a care management team cannot proactively reach out to every patient every month. They need a system that identifies the 300 or 400 patients most likely to have a preventable hospital admission, emergency department visit, or serious clinical deterioration in the next 90 days, so that care coordination resources can be concentrated where they will have the greatest impact. Traditional risk stratification relied on simple actuarial models — patients with the highest total spending in the prior year were assumed to be the highest risk in the coming year. These models are easy to implement but systematically misdirected: they identify patients who were recently sick rather than patients who are about to become sick, missing the early intervention window where care management is most effective and most cost-efficient.

Modern AI-powered risk stratification uses machine learning models trained on large clinical datasets to predict future utilization risk based on a much richer set of signals than historical spending alone. These models incorporate diagnosis trajectories (the sequence and pattern of diagnoses over time, not just their presence or absence), medication adherence signals derived from pharmacy data and EHR medication reconciliation records, laboratory value trends (a gradually rising HbA1c over three visits is a stronger predictor of near-term hospitalization than a single elevated value), social determinants of health flags derived from screening questionnaires and zip-code-level data, and behavioral health diagnoses and substance use disorder flags that are strongly predictive of high-cost medical utilization. The predictive accuracy of leading AI risk stratification models, as measured by the C-statistic — the probability that the model correctly identifies a patient who will be hospitalized as higher risk than a patient who will not — has improved from approximately 0.70 for traditional claims-based models to 0.82–0.87 for the leading AI models that incorporate multi-modal EHR data, a meaningful improvement that translates directly into better care management targeting and higher ROI on care coordinator time.

contentBlocks.heading: The AI Bias Problem: When Risk Stratification Perpetuates Inequity
contentBlocks.body: AI risk stratification tools carry a well-documented and serious equity risk: because they are trained on historical healthcare utilization data, they tend to encode the biases present in that data. A landmark 2019 study published in Science by Obermeyer et al. found that a widely used commercial risk stratification algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it used healthcare costs as a proxy for health need — and because Black patients historically had lower healthcare costs not because they were healthier, but because structural barriers limited their access to care. The algorithm learned that low-cost patients were low-need patients, a correlation that held for white patients but produced systematic underestimation of Black patients’ clinical risk. The practical consequence was that Black patients were significantly less likely to be identified for high-intensity care management programs, perpetuating the very care access disparities that VBC is intended to address. This finding has been replicated for other demographic groups and other algorithm types, establishing AI bias as a genuine and important equity challenge in VBC technology deployment.

contentBlocks.heading: Quote
contentBlocks.body: We audited five commercial risk stratification products used by our ACO network and found that four of them showed statistically significant underestimation of risk for patients in the lowest income quintile. This is not a vendor quality problem — it is a training data problem. If your model learns from utilization data generated in a fee-for-service world with documented access barriers, it will encode those barriers as predicted need. — Ziad Obermeyer, UC Berkeley School of Public Health, NEJM Catalyst, 2025.

contentBlocks.heading: Key Concept
contentBlocks.body: Technology Governance Requirement: Any healthcare organization deploying an AI risk stratification tool in a VBC context has an ethical and, increasingly, a legal obligation to audit the tool for demographic performance disparities before deployment and on a regular basis thereafter. The audit should examine whether the model’s sensitivity and specificity — its ability to correctly identify high-risk and low-risk patients — varies significantly across racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic subgroups. If it does, the organization must either select a different model, recalibrate the existing model for its specific population, or supplement algorithmic risk scoring with clinical and social worker judgment for populations where the algorithm performs poorly.

contentBlocks.heading: Telehealth as a VBC Enabler: The COVID Legacy
contentBlocks.body:
The COVID-19 pandemic produced one technology outcome that has proven durably beneficial for value-based care: the rapid normalization of telehealth as a routine care delivery modality. Between March and June 2020, CMS issued emergency waivers that allowed Medicare to reimburse telehealth visits at parity with in-person visits, removed geographic restrictions that had historically limited telehealth to rural areas, and authorized audio-only visits for patients without video capability. Telehealth utilization increased from approximately 840,000 visits per week in the pre-pandemic baseline to 52 million visits per week at the April 2020 peak, a 6,100% increase in utilization that demonstrated both the latent demand for telehealth and the clinical feasibility of delivering a substantial proportion of primary care and chronic disease management visits via video or phone. For value-based care organizations, telehealth is a care management efficiency multiplier: it allows care coordinators and physicians to conduct follow-up visits, medication reviews, and chronic disease check-ins at a fraction of the cost and scheduling friction of in-person visits, enabling more frequent touchpoints with high-risk patients than would be operationally feasible in a purely in-person model.

The impact of telehealth on VBC care management efficiency is supported by utilization and outcome data from CMS’s post-pandemic evaluation of Medicare telehealth claims, which documents the specific visit types, patient populations, and clinical conditions where telehealth has demonstrated both patient adoption and comparable clinical outcomes to in-person care. This evidence base is directly relevant for VBC organizations making decisions about which components of their care management model to deliver via telehealth versus in person.

The policy question that followed the pandemic’s emergency waivers was whether CMS would make the telehealth flexibilities permanent. The Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 and the CAA of 2024 extended most telehealth flexibilities through 2025, and the Telehealth Modernization Act of 2026 — currently in Senate committee as of March 2026 — would make them permanent for Medicare beneficiaries and extend audio-only coverage as a permanent benefit for patients without access to broadband or video-capable devices. For rural VBC providers, the permanence of telehealth reimbursement parity is not a convenience issue — it is a care model viability issue. An ACO serving a rural population where 40% of attributed patients live more than 30 miles from the nearest primary care office cannot achieve the visit frequency that effective chronic disease management requires without telehealth as a structural component of its care model.

contentBlocks.heading: Building Technology Readiness: The Sequenced Investment Roadmap
contentBlocks.body:
For healthcare leaders assessing their organization’s VBC technology readiness, the most common mistake is attempting to deploy advanced analytics capabilities before the foundational data quality and connectivity infrastructure is in place. A population health platform fed by an EHR with poorly configured structured data will generate inaccurate risk scores. A care gap reporting system connected to an EHR that does not have standardized problem list coding will miss a significant proportion of the gaps it is supposed to identify. Technology investment in VBC should follow a deliberate sequence, with each layer validated before the next layer is added. The following roadmap reflects the sequence used by the highest-performing rural VBC organizations in HTR’s research, based on analysis of MSSP ACO performance data correlated with technology adoption patterns.

Phase 1 — Data Foundation (Months 1–6): Audit your EHR’s structured data quality. Assess the completeness and accuracy of your problem list, medication list, and care gap documentation. Implement standardized coding for diagnoses (ICD-10), medications (RxNorm), and procedures (CPT). This phase produces no new technology capability but is the single most important determinant of all subsequent analytics quality.

Phase 2 — Connectivity (Months 4–12): Activate your state HIE connection and configure admission-discharge-transfer (ADT) alert feeds so that care coordinators receive real-time notifications when attributed patients are admitted to or discharged from any participating hospital in your market. This is the highest-ROI single connectivity investment for ACO care management.

Phase 3 — Panel Management (Months 9–18): Implement a population health management platform that allows care coordinators to view and filter their attributed patient panel by risk level, care gap status, and recent utilization events. At this stage, risk stratification can be claims-based or simple rules-based — AI is not required for effective panel management at this phase.

Phase 4 — Predictive Intelligence (Months 18–36): Implement AI-powered risk stratification once your EHR data quality and HIE connectivity are sufficient to feed the model with the multi-modal data it requires for accurate predictions. Conduct a demographic equity audit of the model before deployment. Begin using model outputs to prioritize care coordinator outreach and track whether high-model-score patients who receive outreach have lower subsequent hospitalization rates than comparable patients who do not.

Phase 5 — Continuous Improvement (Ongoing): Establish a quarterly data quality review cycle that monitors EHR documentation completeness, risk model accuracy, care gap closure rates, and population health outcome trends. Use this data to identify where the care management workflow is breaking down — whether the issue is risk score accuracy, care coordinator capacity, patient engagement, or post-acute care coordination — and address the root cause rather than adjusting the technology.

contentBlocks.heading: Module 4 Summary: Technology Is the Operating System of Value-Based Care
contentBlocks.body:
The technology infrastructure required for effective value-based care is not exotic or cutting-edge by the standards of other industries. What VBC requires is reliable clinical data capture, standards-based data exchange, and analytics capable of turning population data into actionable care management intelligence. These are not science-fiction capabilities. They exist today in mature form at health systems like Kaiser Permanente, Intermountain Healthcare, and Geisinger. The challenge is not invention — it is diffusion. The 34% of rural Critical Access Hospitals that lack the foundational technology capabilities for advanced VBC participation are not being held back by the absence of technology. They are being held back by the absence of capital, broadband infrastructure, and technical implementation support that would allow them to deploy technology that already exists.

The federal investment framework for closing this gap — TEFCA for interoperability standards, the 21st Century Cures Act’s information blocking prohibition and FHIR mandate, the FCC’s Healthcare Connect Fund for rural broadband, ONC’s certification program for EHR capabilities, and HRSA’s rural health IT funding stream — represents the most coherent federal technology infrastructure investment in healthcare history. Whether it is sufficient to close the rural-urban VBC readiness gap within a policy-relevant timeframe is an open question that depends on appropriations decisions, state implementation capacity, and vendor market dynamics that are outside any single organization’s control. What is within your organization’s control is the sequenced technology investment roadmap described in this module, and the commitment to building VBC data infrastructure as a strategic priority rather than an IT project.

VBC technology infrastructure has three interdependent layers: clinical data capture (EHR), data integration and exchange (HIE and FHIR), and analytics and intelligence (population health platforms and AI risk stratification). Each layer depends on the quality of the layer below it, making data foundation investment the highest-priority first step.

The 21st Century Cures Act’s information blocking prohibition and FHIR API mandate are the legal and technical foundations of modern health IT interoperability. Any EHR vendor or health system that restricts data sharing in violation of these provisions faces civil monetary penalties of up to $1 million per violation.

AI risk stratification tools improve high-risk patient identification accuracy significantly compared to claims-based models, but carry documented equity risks from training data bias that require formal demographic audit before deployment and on an ongoing basis.

Telehealth is a structural care model component for rural VBC providers serving populations where in-person visit frequency sufficient for effective chronic disease management is geographically and logistically impossible. The permanence of post-pandemic telehealth reimbursement parity is a VBC infrastructure issue, not simply a convenience policy question.

contentBlocks.heading: Key Concept
contentBlocks.body: Module 4 Key Takeaway: Technology readiness is the most concrete and actionable dimension of VBC preparation because it can be assessed objectively, sequenced rationally, and funded through a combination of organizational capital and federal programs. Before your organization takes on additional VBC financial risk, conduct a structured technology readiness assessment using the capability gap framework from this module and identify which phase of the five-phase roadmap you are currently in. Attempting to manage population cost without the data infrastructure to know who your highest-risk patients are and what is happening to them across the care continuum is the most common cause of VBC financial underperformance — and the most preventable.
